zones.name: A company-run district inside a state
zones.essay:
The idea is to stop trying to leave a country and to become, in law, a small piece of its local government. In the United States and many other places, a state legislature creates counties, cities and special districts, which are public bodies with narrow jobs such as water or roads. A company that owns nearly all the land in one spot can ask for such a body and then fill it with its own people. This combines a claim inside a state, a carve-out granted by a host, and the capture of a town. What comes out is real public power, including taxes, bonds, building codes and sometimes police, held by a private owner in practice.

The largest example is Walt Disney World. Disney bought land near Orlando through shell companies, and on 12 May 1967 Florida's governor signed the law creating the Reedy Creek Improvement District and two cities. The district ran land use, building codes, utilities, roads and fire protection. Votes went to landowners, one per acre, and Disney owned most of the land, so it effectively chose the board. The Florida Supreme Court held in 1968 that the law did not break the state constitution.

Some of this is settled law. American courts apply a rule that each voter counts equally in electing local government, and the United States Supreme Court made a narrow exception in Ball v. James in 1981. There it upheld voting by landowners, weighted by acres, for an Arizona water district, because the district's purpose was specialised and its burdens fell on landowners. It is equally settled that ownership of a town does not remove the rights of the people in it. In Marsh v. Alabama in 1946 a Jehovah's Witness was arrested for handing out leaflets in Chickasaw, a town owned by a shipbuilding company. The Court ruled for her and said that ownership does not always mean absolute dominion. And it is settled that a legislature can undo what it made. Florida voted in April 2022 to dissolve the district. In February 2023 it kept the district under a new name and gave the governor the power to appoint the five board members. Pullman, Illinois, ended the same way in an earlier age, when the state's highest court in 1898 ordered the company to give up the town.

What remains open is narrower than the headlines. Nobody has settled how general a body can be and still keep landowner voting. Ball v. James stressed that the Arizona district was narrow, and Reedy Creek did far more than deliver water, but the 1968 Florida ruling and the 1981 federal case do not answer that for a full city with residents. Disney limited its residents to the two small cities partly from fear that a 1968 case, Avery v. Midland County, would force votes for all residents. The second open point was the agreement Disney and the old board signed just before the state took control, which limited the new board's power and used a clause running until 21 years after the death of the last living descendant of King Charles III. A federal judge ruled against Disney in January 2024 on its suit against the governor, Disney settled the state cases in March 2024, and no court finished deciding whether the agreement was valid.

Now follow the idea through. Suppose a company owns a large tract in a state with a friendly legislature. It first needs a bill, and bills draw neighbours. Blockchains, Inc. owned about 67,000 acres in Storey County, Nevada, and in 2021 wanted a new form of government there, called an Innovation Zone, for a planned 36,000 residents. The governor promoted it in his State of the State address, Storey County objected on money and logistics, critics called it a company town, questions arose about water, and the legislature sent it to a study committee. The company withdrew in October 2021 after saying it had spent more than $300 million in Nevada. A company that does get its district still has every ordinary tie to the state. Its staff are citizens, its bonds are sold under securities law, and federal law applies throughout. Reading the text of these cases, it seems that the power rests on continued political tolerance, and that the size of the project raises the price of removing it. Critics of the 2022 Florida law pointed to more than $1 billion in district bonds.

Small places show how far control can go through housing alone. Vernon, California, is an industrial city founded in 1905 where the city owned nearly all the homes and tenants were mostly city employees or linked to them. It had 112 people in 2010. In 2006 outsiders moved in to run for council, the city cut their power and tried to evict them, and a judge let them run, and they lost. State lawmakers nearly dissolved Vernon in 2011, and the Assembly voted 58 to 7 to do so, before the Senate rejected the bill after Vernon accepted reforms and agreed to set aside $60 million for nearby cities. Criminal charges had already reached its mayor and administrator. Starbase, Texas, is the newest case. Voters there approved a city in May 2025 under ordinary state rules, with a SpaceX vice-president unopposed as mayor. Outside the United States, the Hawksbill Creek Agreement of 1955 let Wallace Groves and the Grand Bahama Port Authority develop and administer Freeport, under terms extended to 2054. A tribunal in March 2026 rejected both the government's $357 million claim and most of the company's counterclaims, including the claim to exclusive authority over the area.

The strongest version is a large landowner with a single friendly legislature, a narrow stated purpose, broad public services and long-term bonds. That can last for generations, as Reedy Creek lasted 56 years and Freeport has lasted 71. It gives local power and no separation from the country. Taxes to the higher government, criminal law and the constitution all continue, and recognition by a foreign state is not part of what this route can produce.

odds.why: Local special districts and company towns are common and lawful, so getting one is realistic for a large landowner with political support. Blockchains shows that a bill can fail even with a governor's backing. Reedy Creek lasted 56 years and then had its board taken over by the state, so a long life is possible while control remains revocable. It stays part of the country, so recognition is close to zero.

rules.says: Upheld voting limited to landowners and weighted by land for a water district with a narrow purpose whose burdens fell on landowners.
A company that owns a town cannot use ownership to stop free speech and religion rights on its streets.

zones.name: Partnering with a tribal nation and its immunity
zones.essay:
Federally recognised Native American tribes hold a kind of authority that no company or town has. American courts call them domestic dependent nations. They govern their own members and territory, and they cannot be sued unless they agree or Congress says so. This is called sovereign immunity, which means a government's protection from being taken to court without its consent. The idea here is that an outside business teams up with a tribe so that the business, or something it owns, sits behind that protection. It combines older Indigenous authority with the carve-out model, using a real government as the partner in place of a host state's special law.

The settled law is firmer than most people expect. In Michigan v. Bay Mills Indian Community in 2014, the United States Supreme Court held that a tribe was immune from a state's suit over a casino the tribe opened on land outside its reservation, and it declined to overturn its rule that immunity reaches off-reservation business. The same opinion marks the limits. The tribes are subject to the plenary control of Congress, meaning Congress can change or end the immunity whenever it chooses. A state may use other mechanisms, including legal actions against the responsible individuals, and tribal members off the reservation are subject to general state law unless federal law says otherwise. So immunity protects the tribal government from one kind of lawsuit, and it does not make conduct lawful or protect the people carrying it out.

Two kinds of real attempt show this. The first is what critics call rent-a-tribe lending. Online lenders charge rates above state limits and say a tribe makes the loans. Courts have divided on the facts, and that division is the live part of the law. In Williams v. Big Picture Loans in 2019, the federal appeals court for the Fourth Circuit said that the business claiming immunity carries the burden of proving it is an arm of the tribe, and it applied a list of factors covering how the business was created, its purpose, control and intent, and the financial tie. It then held the lending companies of the Lac Vieux Desert Band immune, even though the arrangement followed a court loss and an enforcement action against another lender and the tribe at first received 2 percent of gross revenue, with $20 million paid to a company linked to the outside investor by September 2017, against nearly $5 million to the tribe. A later federal court found that facts given to the Fourth Circuit had been misrepresented, according to a report on that ruling. In Gingras v. Think Finance in 2019, the Second Circuit held that tribal officers can be sued for orders stopping violations of state law off tribal land, and that the loan arbitration clauses were unenforceable.

The second attempt was in patents. Allergan transferred its patents on the eye drug Restasis to the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe, and the transfer was recorded on 8 September 2017, while a competitor, Mylan, was challenging them at the Patent Office. The tribe claimed immunity from the review. On 20 July 2018 the Federal Circuit ruled that tribal immunity cannot be asserted in that kind of review, because it is closer to the government reconsidering its own grant than a private lawsuit. The court said that immunity does not bar action by the federal government as the superior sovereign. It decided only that question, and it left open whether state immunity should be treated differently.

What remains open, then, is how much real control and benefit a tribe must have before a business counts as an arm of it, and courts weigh lists of factors with no fixed share or formula. Also open is any use of this for territory. No court has been asked whether a non-Native settlement could live under tribal authority through a business deal. Reading the cases, it seems that immunity attaches to the tribe and to true arms of it, and that it gives an outside founder nothing personal. Nor could a tribe hand over more than it has, and what it has is subject to Congress.

Follow what would really happen. A founder proposes a venture on tribal land. The tribe's own council must agree, and tribal law then governs the venture, so the founder has swapped one government for another and is now a guest. Land bought elsewhere does not turn into Indian land by purchase. When Bay Mills bought property with a federal land claim fund, the Interior Department concluded the property had not become Indian territory, and that was why the state called the casino unlawful. Federal agencies can still act, as the Patent Office case shows, and the founder keeps a personal exposure under state and federal law, since the Bay Mills opinion names responsible individuals as the target. Banks, payment processors and the founder's home country all deal with the founder in person and can apply ordinary rules. Reading the text, a business would also find that outside parties demand a waiver of immunity before lending or contracting, since immunity makes a contract hard to enforce. That last point is general reasoning and is not drawn from a ruling.

The potential is real for a different kind of project. A tribe that owns, runs and profits from a venture on its own land has a lawful and durable form of self-government, and it has done this through casinos under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, which requires a compact with the state for casino gaming on Indian lands. The strongest version is a tribally led zone in which the tribe is truly in charge and outsiders are tenants, within federal law. That is tribal sovereignty working as it does today, and it does not create a new state or give outsiders a way out of the country's law. Foreign recognition is not on offer, since federal law treats tribes as dependent on the United States.

odds.why: Tribal immunity is real and courts have upheld it even for off-reservation business. It belongs to the tribe, Congress can end it, and it does not protect outside individuals. The Federal Circuit refused to apply it to patent review in 2018, and the Second Circuit let suits against tribal officers go ahead in 2019. Money is low because banks and partners are wary of lenders and firms they cannot sue. It cannot lead to foreign recognition of a new state.

zones.name: An investment treaty as a shield
zones.essay:
Most special zones rest on a promise from a government, and governments change. An investment treaty is an agreement between two countries in which each promises fair treatment to investors from the other, and it often lets an investor take a dispute directly to arbitration. Arbitration is a private hearing before appointed judges. The best-known forum is the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes, or ICSID, a World Bank body. The idea here is to add a treaty on top of a zone, so that a later government that cancels the zone must pay for doing so. This combines a host's carve-out with protection from outside the host's own courts.

Some of this is clear. A treaty award is about money, and it does not restore a zone or give anyone a right to rule. Using the forum also requires consent, which comes from a treaty or a contract, because ICSID membership alone gives no investor a right to sue. Enforcement has real force, since member countries agree to treat an award like a ruling of their own courts. A country that repeals a scheme investors relied on can lose. Romania adopted investment incentives for certain regions in 1999, and investors built a large food business relying on them. Romania repealed them as part of joining the European Union, and in 2013 a tribunal found a breach of the Romania and Sweden treaty and awarded about £70 million plus interest. The European Commission then ruled that paying the award would be illegal state aid. The European General Court annulled that ruling in 2019, and in 2020 the United Kingdom Supreme Court unanimously lifted a stay so that enforcement could proceed in England. The dispute went on in the EU courts after that, and one later ruling of the General Court is reported to have again treated the award as state aid.

The live test is Próspera. It is a private zone on the island of Roatán, set up under the Honduran law on Zones for Employment and Economic Development, or ZEDEs. In April 2022 Honduras repealed the law, and on 20 September 2024 its Supreme Court declared the laws unconstitutional from the start. The owners filed Honduras Próspera Inc. and others v. Honduras, ICSID case ARB/23/2, relying on CAFTA-DR, the trade treaty linking the United States with Central America, and on a legal stability agreement with the state. The first demand was $10.775 billion, later reported as reduced to about $1.63 billion. Honduras left ICSID in 2024 and rejoined with effect from 16 August 2026, and the case was still pending in October 2026.

The open questions here are the ones that matter. No tribunal has yet ruled in the Próspera case on whether a promise made under a law later held void from the start can found a treaty claim. The Honduran Supreme Court's ruling treats the zones as never lawful, and the investors rely on promises the state made to them. President Castro's government described ending the zones as recovering sovereignty, and critics and supporters disagree over whether a claim of this kind should exist at all. Paul Romer, an economist who first promoted charter cities, has said Próspera is not close to a model he would recommend. A second open case has appeared in Australia. Landbridge, a Chinese company that holds a 99-year lease of the Port of Darwin, is reported to have filed at ICSID in May 2026 to stop what it calls a forced sale, after both main parties promised in 2025 to return the port to Australian ownership. How that ends is not known. Panama's Supreme Court ruled in January 2026 that the contracts for two canal ports held by a CK Hutchison company were unconstitutional, and the company said it would go to arbitration.

Follow the steps. An investor needs the nationality of a country with a treaty, so the founders' passports and the place where the company is registered begin to matter. Next the host must agree to a stability contract or already have a treaty in force. When a later government moves against the zone, the investor files, and hearings run for years while legal costs mount. During that time local courts and police keep their powers, because a tribunal cannot order officers off the land. Reading the awards, it seems that the treaty shifts the cost of cancelling onto the state and leaves the decision with the state. Banks and insurers can take comfort from a treaty only as far as they believe an award can be collected, and Micula shows collection can take more than a decade after a 2005 filing.

The Sulu heirs' case shows a nearby failure. Eight claimants won a $14.92 billion award against Malaysia on an 1878 contract, and French courts undid it because the arbitrator lacked power. That case turned on whether Malaysia had ever agreed to the arbitrator, so the terms of consent decide whether any of this protection exists.

The route does have potential as a financial deterrent against a poor host, and that deterrent may buy time and a negotiated outcome. The strongest version is a clear treaty between two states, a specific stability contract signed by the proper authority, and a project built so that local people want it to continue. Even that version produces money or a settlement, and the land remains the host's. It has never produced recognition of anything as a state.

odds.why: Investors do win such claims, as in Micula, so the legal tool is real. It delivers money after many years and cannot order a state to keep a zone. Próspera is still operating with its case pending, which shows some protection, and no ruling on the merits exists. Honduras's court has already voided the underlying law. It adds nothing to recognition.

zones.name: Association with a larger state
zones.essay:
Free association is an arrangement in which a small place runs itself while a larger state handles some of the jobs of a country, usually defence and part of its foreign relations. A new founder could imagine using it as a halfway house. A territory would get self-government from a host, the host would keep the expensive duties, and outside governments might gradually deal with the place as a state. This combines a carve-out, the end of colonial rule, and an international agreement.

The working models are clear. The Cook Islands have been self-governing in free association with New Zealand since 4 August 1965, and Niue since 19 October 1974. New Zealand cannot make laws for them, and it acts on defence and foreign affairs only when they ask. They have their own immigration rules, and their people hold New Zealand citizenship. Each signs United Nations treaties and joins UN bodies as a state, the Cook Islands since 1992 and Niue since 1994. Neither is a UN member. The Compact states with the United States went further. The Marshall Islands and Micronesia, associated in 1986, and Palau, associated in 1994, are independent states, and the United States provides money and defence and holds control over who may bring forces in. The Marshall Islands and Micronesia are UN members.

What is open is the legal character of the relationship, and it is argued now. Free association by itself does not decide whether a place is a state. In 2025 the Cook Islands' prime minister, Mark Brown, said the UN had confirmed that his country did not meet membership requirements, and its foreign minister said joining would need a referendum and a new look at the tie to New Zealand. A New Zealand foreign ministry spokesperson said that the Cook Islands is not a fully independent and sovereign state, and New Zealand has said UN membership could cost its people automatic access to New Zealand citizenship. Each document is specific to its parties, so there is no general rule for how a place leaves. The Caribbean associated states of the 1960s asked for and received independence, and Anguilla broke away from one of them and went back to Britain as a dependent territory.

Now consider a founder trying this today. A private group has no territory with a claim to self-government, so it would first need a host's carve-out, and then a constitutional change by the host. Every existing association grew out of a place already under a colonial or trust arrangement, and reading the record it seems the path has been open to peoples and territories, with no example of a private settlement using it. That is an inference from the list of cases and not a rule stated in a treaty. The attempts inside modern states have mostly failed. Spain's Congress of Deputies rejected a Basque proposal in 2003, and the Philippine Supreme Court struck down a Bangsamoro proposal in 2008. Tatarstan's 1994 treaty of association with Russia was overtaken by constitutional changes in 2002. Voters in the Cocos (Keeling) Islands in 1984 had the option and 21 of 261 chose it. Tokelau's referendums of 2006 and 2007 failed to reach the two-thirds needed.

Follow what it would mean in practice. The larger partner's passports would likely be the first thing residents want, and the Cook Islands' experience shows how tightly that ties them to the partner's decisions. The larger state also stays answerable abroad, so it would keep some control over who enters and which treaties the place signs. The Compacts show the price, since the United States holds authority over defence and in return pays large sums. The 2003 renewal gave Micronesia and the Marshall Islands $3.5 billion. A new place would have to offer something worth that, such as a strategic location, and few private projects can. Banks and telecoms would likely deal with it through the partner's systems, which reading the arrangements seems the natural result, though a new case would set its own terms.

The potential is small and specific. The strongest version is an existing autonomous territory with a real population that negotiates association after a referendum, with a private developer as a junior partner. Reaching treaty capacity through a long tie, as the Cook Islands did from 1965 to 1992, is the part of this path that actually has a record. It is a route for peoples who are already there, and it takes decades.

odds.why: The Cook Islands and the Compact states show that association works and can last for generations. All grew out of colonial or trust territories, and no private settlement has used it. A host would have to change its constitution for a new place. Recognition can follow, as it did for the Marshall Islands and Micronesia, but only for an existing people.

rules.says: Self-government in free association, with New Zealand acting on defence and foreign affairs only when asked.

zones.name: A long lease from a small state
zones.essay:
The idea is to approach a small country with little money and much land or sea, such as Kiribati or Vanuatu, and offer to pay for a long lease with special terms. Small governments may need income, and a project could seem to offer jobs. It combines a lease with a purchase attempt and a carve-out. People ask about Pacific countries most often for this.

The legal basics are settled. A lease gives the right to use land for a period, and the land and the right to govern stay with the country. A lease is also only as good as the authority of whoever signs it. In September 2019 the premier of Central Province in the Solomon Islands signed an agreement giving a Chinese developer, China Sam, exclusive development rights to Tulagi and neighbouring islands. The national attorney-general soon declared it unlawful and unenforceable, because the province lacked the power and required reviews had not happened. A deal with one official or one part of a government can be undone by another part.

The record of private founders in the Pacific is short. Anton Bakov's Romanov Empire project talked with Kiribati about buying land, and by 2017 those talks had failed. Wirtland, an internet project, announced in 2010 that it had approached Nauru about a transfer, and no land is known to have changed hands. On Lataro Island in Vanuatu, a British resident held a 75-year lease and in 2022 began selling plots and citizenship as digital tokens under the name Satoshi Island. A lease is not ownership, so he could not sell land outright, and Vanuatu's government said a token gave no right of residence. In July 2025 the company said its assets could no longer be traded because of a breach of the land lease. Vanuatu has its own history with such plans. In 1980 the American Phoenix Foundation put money behind Vemerana, a breakaway state on the island of Santo, hoping for a tax haven, and the attempt did not survive independence.

Kiribati shows what a small state's own priorities look like. Its government bought 2,210 hectares in Fiji in 2014 for $8.6 million, as protection against climate change. That land remains under Fijian law. Its president also spoke in 2011 of floating islands costing about $2 billion, to be paid for by other countries.

What is open is how much a small state could legally grant by its own law to a long-term lessee. Nothing stops a sovereign state from passing a statute giving a zone tax breaks, its own rules and even its own courts, as the United Arab Emirates did for the Dubai International Financial Centre and as Laos did in a commercial form for the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone, a 99-year lease of 10,000 hectares. Whether any given Pacific constitution would permit it is a question for each country's own courts, and it has not been tested for a sovereignty-like grant. Reading the examples, it seems that a small state can give a lot within its own law, and that it cannot give what is not its own to give, such as the agreement of other governments to treat the zone as separate. The Golden Triangle shows the outside reach. In 2018 the United States Treasury placed sanctions on the company behind it, which is a measure Washington can apply through banks whatever the Lao lease says.

Follow the steps. A founder negotiates with ministers and has to show money. A long lease then goes through lawyers, and local land interests can decide the outcome, as Vanuatu's own history shows, since the Nagriamel movement on Santo grew out of demands for unused European-held land to return to islanders. Satoshi Island's lease was the single thing all buyers depended on. A new government might see the deal differently, and foreign neighbours may take an interest. Tulagi drew attention from Western diplomats within weeks, because deep harbours in the Pacific interest navies. Residents would still need visas and passports from somewhere, and a port and an airline connection through the host. Payment flows would run through the host's banks, which keep links with overseas correspondent banks only by following international rules.

The strongest version is a real lease of modest scale, approved by the national legislature with local owners in agreement, offering a zone under the host's law and clear benefits to local people. That can work for decades. It gives its holder the position of a tenant under a friendly government, with an end date, and nothing further.

odds.why: Long leases from small states exist, as at Lataro Island and in Laos, so getting one is possible. Tulagi and Satoshi Island show how easily one fails. Bakov's and Wirtland's approaches for land gave no result. The grant lasts as long as the host's politics allow, and a tenant under a host's law does not gain recognition.

zones.name: A state ceding land by treaty to a new body
zones.essay:
The cleanest legal route to a new territory would be this. An existing state signs a treaty handing a piece of its land to a new body, gives up all claim to it, and the new body becomes its government. Title would then come from the one party entitled to give it. This combines buying from a state, an agreement between governments, and the attempt to become a state.

Some of this is clear. States can transfer territory to each other. Tiran and Sanafir went from Egypt to Saudi Arabia after an announcement in 2016. Sovereignty over Vatican City was recognised to the Holy See by Italy in the Lateran Treaty of 1929, creating a state of 44 hectares. It is also clear that treaties are made between entities with capacity. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, in Article 6, says every state has the capacity to make them. It says nothing that helps a company or club. And it is clear that a transfer from one state does not bind other states to recognise the result. South Africa declared four homelands independent from 1976, starting with Transkei, and no other government accepted them.

The hard part is the recipient. The Holy See was an old international body with diplomatic ties before 1929, and its case is not a pattern for a new group. The closest modern parallel is the 1998 treaty by which Malta gave the Order of Malta, another old body with diplomatic ties, use of part of Fort St Angelo for 99 years. It gave the Order use with listed privileges and it did not give sovereignty. What is open, and has not been tested, is whether a brand-new private body could receive sovereignty directly by treaty. Nothing in the Vienna Convention says that it could never hold title, since a place may become a state by meeting the usual tests of territory, population and government. Reading the text, it seems that a treaty signed with a body that is not yet a state would at first count as a domestic act of the giving state or as a private contract, and that the new place's status would depend on other governments' responses. That reasoning is a reading and no court has ruled on it.

Politics makes the transfer far harder than the law. In the Tiran and Sanafir case, a transfer between two friendly states set off the largest protests of the Egyptian president's time in office, with hundreds arrested. The Chagos treaty shows how slow it can be, even when a court has spoken. In 2019 the International Court of Justice advised that Britain should end its rule of the islands. On 22 May 2025 Britain and Mauritius signed a treaty transferring sovereignty and letting Britain exercise rights on Diego Garcia for an initial 99 years, for annual payments. Then a change in the American position stalled it, the British bill lapsed in April 2026, and as of October 2026 it was not in force. The same opinion shows a further limit. The court held that Mauritius's agreement to give up the islands in 1965 was not valid, because it came while Britain ruled Mauritius, and that land cannot be split off without the free and genuine will of the people concerned. Reading that reasoning, a founder would have to expect the people on any ceded land to have a say, and a deal that ignored them would be open to attack.

Follow the steps. A government must first want this, which means something large in exchange and few voters who object. Its constitution may forbid giving up land, as the Honduran Supreme Court said of an earlier special zone plan on grounds of sovereignty. A parliament must vote, and a later government may attack the treaty. Neighbours with interests in the area would then respond. If it all succeeded, the new place would hold land and would need everything else, including a passport other states accept, a country code, a bank that will deal with it and recognition. The founders would remain citizens of their home countries, with those countries' tax and criminal laws still following them, until they gave up that nationality.

It has potential only as a very rare event. The strongest version would be a state already willing to give up a remote, unpopulated and undisputed piece of land, to a body with real backing from other governments, perhaps as part of a settlement of a bigger problem. No such transfer to a new private body has taken place in modern times. If one did, the title would be strong, which explains the high legal and holding figures.

odds.why: A treaty transfer from a willing state would give the best title of any route. No state is known to have done this for a new private body in modern times. Transfers even between states can cause protests or stall, as with Tiran and the Chagos. If it happened the land would be hard to attack, but recognition would still depend on other states.

rules.cite: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, Art. 6

zones.name: Buying land first, then seeking a cession
zones.essay:
Here the order of events is the point. A group buys ordinary private land in a country and only later asks the government to hand over the right to rule it. The hope is that ownership gives a stronger position to bargain from. This combines a purchase with a later carve-out or transfer, and it is different from a treaty cession because the land is already in the founders' hands when they ask.

The basic rule is settled and easy to state. Buying land gets ownership, and the seller's government keeps the right to rule. A Russian businessman's project that went shopping for territory, the Romanov Empire, met this rule, and so did Kiribati when it bought 2,210 hectares in Fiji for $8.6 million, a purchase that left Fijian law in force. Private land sits inside a legal system, so a deed depends on the very government the owner would want to replace. The Dutch purchase of Manhattan and the American case of Johnson v. M'Intosh in 1823, in which a private buyer's title from Native sellers lost to a government title, show the point from opposite ends of history.

History does hold examples in which purchase led to the right to rule. The clearest is Liechtenstein. Its princely family bought the lordship of Schellenberg for 115,000 guilders in 1699 and the county of Vaduz for 290,000 guilders in 1712, because only rulers of land held directly under the emperor could sit in the Imperial Diet. In 1719 the emperor joined them into a principality, and sovereignty came in 1806. James Brooke in Sarawak and the British North Borneo Company ruled under grants from sultans in the 1800s. The Clunies-Ross family held the Cocos Islands for generations. These grants came from rulers who could give such rights under the rules of their time and who answered to few voters.

A modern version looks different, and it shows up in the land itself. Huang Nubo's 2011 bid for about 300 square kilometres of Iceland needed an exemption, because Icelandic law bars large purchases by buyers from outside the European Economic Area, and the bid collapsed. A large foreign purchase can therefore fail before any question of ruling arises. Douglas Tompkins bought huge areas of Patagonia and gave much of it to the state for parks, so the path he found ran in the opposite direction. The nearest modern success of a land purchase leading to a special legal status is the United Nations site in New York. William Zeckendorf bought the land in 1946, John D. Rockefeller Jr. paid for it, and it was donated to the UN that December, and a treaty with the United States then set the district's status. There the status came because the recipient was an organisation of states.

What is open is whether long ownership and residence can strengthen a later request. No rule says that it does. Territorial title in international law is about states, and the Island of Palmas arbitration of 1928 treated the continuous and peaceful display of the functions of a state as being as good as a title. Reading that, it seems that private ownership counts for little in that test, since a landowner shows no state authority, and that an owner who tried to display it would be breaking the host's law. Hutt River in Australia is the nearest long test. The family held farmland for decades and claimed independence, and Australia never accepted it. Whether any government would ever respond to an established private community with a cession remains unanswered, because none has.

Follow the steps. The group buys through a company, which pays taxes and files reports in the host country. Local planning law applies, and the project must get its permits. As it grows, it becomes a local political issue, as Crawfish Rock's fears became a national issue for Próspera in Honduras. If it asks for a special zone, it becomes a carve-out, with the fragility that implies. If it asks for a full transfer, the government has to overcome its constitution and its voters. Banks and insurers treat the land as ordinary property until then. If founders declare independence before the government agrees, they risk losing what they own, because the courts that protect the deed are the courts they reject.

It has some potential in its first half. Owning land is a solid base for a community, and it gives a lasting place in a local economy, as at Orania in South Africa, an Afrikaner town that about 40 families bought in 1990 and hold through a company, which the government has generally left alone. The strongest full version would be a large owner, in a remote and thinly settled place, that first earns a special zone, and then decades later negotiates more. Reaching the end of that path is very unlikely, and no modern case has done it.

odds.why: Buying land is easy and many groups have done it. Turning it into the right to rule worked only in earlier centuries, as in Liechtenstein and Sarawak, when rulers could give such rights. No modern government has done this for private owners. If one ever did, the result would be fairly secure, so the conditional figures are moderate while the build figure is very low.

zones.name: A headquarters agreement as a model of immunity
zones.essay:
International organisations have offices in ordinary cities, and the host government agrees not to interfere with them. This is done through a headquarters agreement, a treaty or similar document setting out what the host's police, courts and tax officers may and may not do on those premises. Someone looking for a safe legal position might ask whether a new body could get such a deal, and hold land under it. This combines an extraterritorial spot with an international agreement and the idea of an authority that exists without a territory.

The text of these deals is clear, and the most common belief about them is wrong. People often say that UN headquarters is not on American soil. Section 7 of the 1947 agreement says the district is under the control and authority of the United Nations, and that the federal, state and local law of the United States applies inside it, except as the agreement says otherwise. Section 8 lets the UN make regulations for its work, and an American law that conflicts with them does not apply. Section 9 says the district is inviolable, and American officers may enter to perform official duties only with the consent of the Secretary-General. People who break UN rules may be expelled, and further penalties or arrest depend on American law. The United States also keeps its general control over who enters the country, beyond the transit rights the agreement gives, and in 2025 it refused visas to Palestinian Authority officials. Iran and Russia have argued that this control lets Washington influence the General Assembly's work.

The International Committee of the Red Cross is the most relevant example because it is not an organisation of states. It is a private association under Swiss law that has an international role under the Geneva Conventions. In its agreement with Switzerland of 19 March 1993, the Swiss Federal Council recognises its international juridical personality. Its premises cannot be entered without its consent, it has immunity from legal process and from enforcement with some listed exceptions, and it is exempt from most taxes. Switzerland passed a general law, the Host State Act of 2007, under which it can grant such privileges case by case. Those named as beneficiaries include the World Economic Forum, GAVI and the Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue. CERN, the European physics laboratory founded by a convention of 12 states in 1953 to 1954, shows what such a body can do with land. Its site at Meyrin runs across the border, and the French side is under Swiss jurisdiction.

These immunities can be narrowed. In Jam v. International Finance Corporation in 2019, the United States Supreme Court held that international organisations have the same immunity that foreign governments have today, which leaves room for suits over commercial activity. It also noted that an organisation's charter can provide something different, because the statute supplies default rules. Farmers and fishermen in India, who had sued a World Bank lender over a power plant, therefore won on that question, and whether their suit could go on under the commercial activity rule was left open.

What is open is whether a new, non-state group could get this treatment. The Swiss law and the Red Cross example show it can be done for a body doing work a government values. Nothing says a host must do so, and no such agreement is known to cover a body whose purpose is to govern residents. Reading these texts, it seems the immunities are functional, meaning they exist so that an organisation can do a particular job, and that they do not make the land into a separate country. A UN premises is inviolable and the land still belongs within New York's legal system. Whether such a grant could expand to a community with homes, families and births is untested.

Follow the path. A founder would first need a mission that a host wants, such as humanitarian, scientific or standards work, and a track record. Then a foreign ministry would negotiate with it. The deal would likely cover offices and staff, and each exception, such as traffic fines and social insurance at the Red Cross, shows the host keeping small powers. Staff keep their nationality and, unless a deal covers it, their taxes at home. A host can also say it bears no responsibility for the body's acts, as Article 20 of the Red Cross agreement does. Above all, the host can withdraw or decline to renew. The people who work there can still be charged for crimes when the head of the organisation waives immunity, as Kofi Annan did for three officials in 2005 in the Oil-for-Food case.

As a model this has real worth, but it is a model of protected premises. Its strongest version is a respected private body with a useful job, holding a modest campus under a host's law with inviolable buildings. That could be long-lasting and stable. A community that wanted its own courts and citizenship would be asking for something none of these agreements has ever provided.

odds.why: Swiss law and the Red Cross agreement show that non-state bodies can get immunity by agreement. Hosts give it for a valued job, so a body that only wants to govern itself is unlikely to get it. Once made, these agreements have lasted for decades with very few breaches. They protect premises and functions, and they do not create a state, though a body can gain standing in time.

rules.says: The district is under UN control, US law applies unless the agreement says otherwise, and US officers need the Secretary-General's consent to enter.

International organisations in the US have the same immunity as foreign governments today, which excludes much commercial activity, unless a charter says otherwise.
Switzerland may grant immunity, tax exemption and other privileges to international organisations and some other bodies, case by case.

zones.name: A data embassy on a foreign host's soil
zones.essay:
A data embassy is a room of computers in a friendly country that holds a state's records, protected by agreement in much the way an embassy is. The purpose is that the state's records survive if its own territory is attacked. For a digital community with no land, the idea is attractive, since a digital country's real assets are its records. This combines a digital project with an extraterritorial spot and with the old idea of a government that can continue from abroad.

The working examples are few and all rest on a treaty between governments. Estonia signed its agreement with Luxembourg in 2017 and in June 2019 moved four core databases there, with more to follow, including land and business registries. Monaco signed its agreement on 15 July 2021, and Luxembourg's parliament approved it on 9 November 2022. Under the Monaco deal, the premises are exempt from search, requisition, attachment or execution, and no Luxembourg official, including police and judges, may enter without approval from Monaco's representative, except in an emergency such as a fire. The law firm that reported this describes it as Luxembourg's third data embassy, after the European Patent Organisation and Estonia. Lithuania was later reported to be setting one up.

Part of the law is simply clear. The Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations covers embassies, and the Estonian government describes its data centre as an extension of the state in the cloud, drawing on that treaty though not being an embassy in the traditional sense. The protection binds the host, because the host signed. It does not bind other states. A private company can rent space anywhere and encrypt its data, but the servers then sit under local law, and local police and courts can act on them. Nothing lets a project grant itself this protection.

What is open is the legal character of the data embassy itself. Estonia calls it something new under international law, and no court has tested such premises, so how a judge would treat the immunity if a third party sued is unknown. The European Patent Organisation's example suggests that the status is not strictly limited to states, since it is an international organisation made up of states. Reading these facts, it seems that a host could by its own choice give similar treatment to a non-state body, in the way that Switzerland's Host State Act lets it decide case by case who receives privileges. No such deal is known to exist for a private community or a self-declared country. A government wanting to keep good relations with others would have reason to ask who the guest is first.

Follow what a digital country would actually meet. It would approach a host, and the host's foreign ministry would ask what legal person it is dealing with. A body with no recognition has no standing to sign a treaty, so the arrangement would be a contract with a data company, under that company's terms and the local courts. Those terms include obedience to court orders. The Swedish Pirate Party's plan to host The Pirate Bay in 2010 hoped to use parliamentary immunity, and the plan needed seats the party did not win. The people running the project would remain under the laws of their countries, wherever the servers stood. Even an inviolable server room can be cut off, because it depends on the host's electricity and network. Sanctions and export rules on hardware continue to apply to the company that buys the machines. The data embassy protects the records and offers nothing to the people.

Its real potential is modest but practical. For a recognised small state, particularly one threatened by climate or invasion, it is a tested tool. Tuvalu's plan to preserve itself digitally as seas rise reflects that same concern. For an exile government or a recognised non-state body, a friendly host might one day offer something like it. The strongest version for a non-state project would be a respected organisation, already holding a host's immunity under a law like Switzerland's, adding its records to premises already protected. That would protect a register. A digital body with no recognition can realistically expect a good data centre and encryption, and a contract under ordinary law.

odds.why: Estonia and Monaco have these by treaty, so the tool works for states. Non-state versions have not been done and a host has little reason to offer one to an unrecognised body. Running servers is cheap, so money is fairly good. Protected records can last long, but having one does not make anyone recognise a new state.

rules.says: Premises are exempt from search, requisition, attachment and execution, and Luxembourg officials need approval to enter except in emergencies.
Estonian servers in Luxembourg stay under Estonian control with immunity from local seizure.

zones.name: Religious or church status over land
zones.essay:
Religious bodies have held land under special rules for centuries, and governments often treat them with care. This route asks whether a religious identity can add to a territorial claim, through a state's respect for a church, through a tax exemption, or through a religious community running its own town. It combines a host's carve-out, a takeover of local government, and a long-standing authority that does not rest on territory.

Three famous cases are often quoted, and each differs from what a new founder would have. Vatican City became a state in 1929, when Italy recognised the Holy See's sovereignty over 44 hectares in the Lateran Treaty, after a dispute lasting about 60 years. The Holy See had been a ruler and a diplomatic presence for centuries, and it has no modern imitator. Mount Athos in Greece has monks who govern a 335-square-kilometre peninsula, with monasteries dating back to at least the 9th century, under Greek law and with a church link to the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople. It stays part of Greece. The Order of Malta has diplomatic relations with more than 110 countries, and it signed a treaty with Malta in 1998 for part of Fort St Angelo. Its origins go back to about 1099. Age and the consent of states are what these three share.

The law in the United States is clear in one direction. The Constitution bars government from establishing a religion, and the Supreme Court has applied that to local power. In Larkin v. Grendel's Den in 1982 it struck down a Massachusetts law letting churches veto liquor licences nearby. In Board of Education of Kiryas Joel v. Grumet in 1994 it struck down a New York statute that created a special school district following the lines of a village of Satmar Hasidim. Four justices wrote that this delegated state power to a group defined by common religion, and the Court's majority held that the law went beyond accommodating religion. A state may not hand civic authority to a group chosen by a religious test.

Here comes the point that is more open. Kiryas Joel's village itself was formed under New York's general village law, with boundaries drawn to take in only Satmars, and the Court's decision was aimed at the special school statute. Rajneeshpuram went further. The followers of Bhagwan Rajneesh bought 64,281 acres in Oregon in 1981 for $5.75 million and voted a city into being in May 1982. Oregon's attorney general argued that a city whose land and government lay with one religious group merged church and state. A federal judge ruled against the city in 1985, too late to matter, because criminal cases had ended the commune. So a religious community can use general laws to form a town, and whether its town survives depends on how far government and religion have fused. Courts decide that by the facts, and the line is not exact.

Colorado City in Arizona, with Hildale over the Utah border, shows the facts of a fusion over decades. A real estate trust of the Fundamentalist Latter-day Saints owned most of the land, and the town was incorporated in 1985. Arizona and Utah began dismantling the church's ownership in 2007. In July 2012 the Justice Department sued, saying the town government and police were taking orders from the church. In 2014 a jury found the towns had discriminated against a family that were not members and awarded $5.2 million. The population fell from 4,821 in 2010 to 2,478 in 2020.

Follow how it plays out for a new religious founder. Registering as a church may bring tax exemption, depending on the country, and it does not bring territory. The community buys land and is subject to zoning and building law. If it forms a municipality, its officers must serve everyone, and non-members who move in have rights, as the jury's award to a non-member family in Colorado City showed. Children raise special concerns for child welfare authorities, who keep their full power within religious communities. Citizenship, passports and taxes on members stay with their home countries.

Reading the record, it seems that religious status can win patience from a government and that it cannot substitute for the government's consent. That patience can be real. Greek law's treatment of Athos and Italy's treaty with the Holy See show what a very old religious institution can keep. Outside the United States, a state with an official religion could in principle grant a religious body far more than American law would allow, and this has not been tried for a new group in modern times.

The strongest version is a community that keeps its religious life private, forms no government, and owns land as a charity or company under ordinary law. It can then build a very separate way of life and last for generations, as Mount Athos shows at the far end. Recognition as a state is possible for the Holy See only because of a history no new group has.

odds.why: Religious communities can buy land and form towns under general law, so getting established is common. American courts have struck down grants of power based on religion, as in Kiryas Joel and Rajneeshpuram. Colorado City shows long survival followed by state action. Vatican City and Mount Athos rest on old histories that a new group cannot copy, so recognition is close to zero.

rules.cite: Board of Education of Kiryas Joel v. Grumet, 512 U.S. 687 (1994)
rules.says: A special school district drawn for a religious village violated the US Constitution's bar on establishing religion.
A state may not give churches veto power over liquor licences.
Italy recognised the Holy See's sovereignty over Vatican City.

zones.name: A free zone with a private charter
zones.essay:
A special economic zone is an area with lighter rules on tax and trade. Countries have many of them, and on their own they are ordinary economic policy. The idea here goes one step further, by joining the zone to a private charter that gives a company or a council its own courts, its own regulators and control of daily government. It combines a host's carve-out with a lease and with the chartered companies of older times.

The economist Paul Romer popularised the term charter city in a 2009 talk. In his version, a host country gives responsibility for a new city to a more developed trustee country, so that good rules can start fresh and people can choose by moving there. Honduras took up the idea and then changed it. An earlier plan for Special Development Regions was struck down as a breach of sovereignty, and in 2013 the country changed its constitution to allow ZEDEs, zones with their own laws, courts and taxes, without a supervising foreign government. Romer chaired a transparency committee and resigned in September 2012, when the government agency signed with developers without involving it. Próspera, built by a fund manager through a Delaware company, later offered single-digit taxes and a court of retired Arizona judges hearing cases online.

The law here is settled at the level of each country. A host can grant such zones if its constitution allows, and its own top court decides that. The Honduran Supreme Court declared the ZEDE laws unconstitutional on 20 September 2024, with retroactive effect. The grant can also be limited. In the United Arab Emirates, the Dubai International Financial Centre, 110 hectares, has common-law courts for civil and commercial matters since 2006, and federal criminal law and immigration rules still apply inside it. That design has held, because it asks for less.

A long private charter also has history behind it. Under the Hawksbill Creek Agreement of 1955 in the Bahamas, a private port authority built and has administered Freeport under terms extended to 2054, and a tribunal in 2026 rejected its claim of exclusive authority. In Laos, the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone is a 99-year lease of 10,000 hectares run by a Hong Kong-registered group, with its own immigration checkpoint on Lao soil. The Shanghai International Settlement, from 1854 to 1943, is the largest example ever of foreign merchants governing a city. Its council was elected by foreign taxpayers, ran the police and utilities, and governed more than a million people by 1925. Its own regulations said the land remained Chinese territory. It rested on treaties that China had been forced to sign after war, and a settlement of that kind could not be made today, since it depended on foreign military power.

What is open is how much of a state's judicial and legislative power can be delegated under a constitution, and how durable a charter is once elections change the government. The answers differ by country, and few have been tested. Romer and others also disagree about the design itself. Critics called even his trustee model neo-colonial, and he has come to say that Próspera is more like a gated community than the model he would recommend. Reading the experience so far, it seems that zones limited to commercial law last longer than zones claiming general government, though the sample is small.

Follow the steps. A company proposes the zone to a government and a law is drafted. Neighbours and local politicians respond, as at Crawfish Rock on Roatán. A company needs a bank, and banks ask whether a zone's own regulator is respected abroad, which is why such places try to borrow respected legal systems. A criminal law gap would usually be filled by national police, so private guards are a limited substitute. Sanctions show the outside reach. The United States Treasury listed the Golden Triangle's company in 2018, whatever the Lao lease promised. Tax treaties and passports remain those of the host and of residents' own countries.

The strongest version has a narrow scope, such as commercial law and tax, in a stable host where the courts have approved the law before any building begins, with a clear plan for local people. It can bring real investment and a real difference in daily rules for business. It leaves the place inside the host's borders and under the host's final word.

odds.why: Many countries have such zones, and Dubai's has worked since 2006 with its own commercial courts. Wider grants have proved fragile, as Honduras's court showed in 2024. Freeport has lasted since 1955 under contract. The figures sit close to those for host carve-outs, with slightly lower holding odds because a private charter draws more political opposition.

rules.says: Declared the ZEDE laws unconstitutional with retroactive effect.

The settlement's land remained Chinese territory, subject to China's sovereign rights.

zones.name: A pop-up city moving among countries
zones.essay:
A pop-up city is a temporary community where people who met online live together for weeks or months, usually at a resort or a rented campus. The idea of rotating is that a community could keep moving from one country to another, so that it has a continuing membership and culture but depends on no single host. This combines a digital community with short stays in friendly places and with the older notion of a country that has no land. Its followers often link it to the network state, Balaji Srinivasan's plan set out in 2022, in which an online group forms first, buys scattered land and later seeks diplomatic recognition.

The legal position of the real events is plain. Zuzalu, about 200 people at Lustica Bay in Montenegro for about two months from 25 March 2023, took no land and made no new law, and everyone stayed under Montenegrin law. Edge Esmeralda in Healdsburg, California, had about 1,300 people in 2024 under ordinary American law. Zuitzerland in Laax in the Swiss Alps and ShanhaiWoo, which has met in China and Thailand, are other examples. Vitalia in February 2024 borrowed a different legal footing by meeting inside Próspera in Honduras. The Network School in a hotel at Forest City in Malaysia became permanent in May 2025, and in law it was a business with a council licence under Malaysian rules. On 21 July 2026 the Iskandar Puteri City Council revoked that licence and ordered it to stop the next day, after a public row in which commentators objected to its stated aims on sovereignty. Kazakhstan's digital ministry signed a non-binding memorandum within hours, and a campus opened in Astana on 2 September 2026. Each participant needs permission to enter the host country, and each stays subject to the host's law while there.

There is nothing unlawful about gathering, and none of these events has claimed sovereignty. Moving does not create a legal status. International law knows no category of state that travels, and the tests in the Montevideo Convention include a defined territory. Reading these rules, it seems that a rotating community is, in law, a series of ordinary visits plus some kind of organisation registered somewhere.

What is open is mostly outside courts. No one knows yet whether long rotation could build a body that governments treat with some standing, the way the Order of Malta kept its diplomatic ties after losing its island in 1798. The Order's standing came from centuries of history, and its case is not a pattern for a new group. A separate open point is taxation. Staying a short time in each country may avoid becoming a tax resident in any of them under each country's own day-counting rules, while the home country of an American, for one, continues to tax on the basis of citizenship. Which country's rules apply to a person who moves all year depends on national rules and tax treaties, and has not been tested for such a group. Reading the rules, a person may simply remain a tax resident of their last home.

Follow what would happen in practice. The organisers sign contracts with a hotel or a landowner in the host, under local law. Participants arrive on tourist or business visas. Those who work remotely on tourist stays may be breaking the terms of their entry in some countries, and the host decides whether to look away. A clinic offering an experimental treatment, the theme of Zuzalu's longevity track, faces local medical rules, which is why Vitalia chose Próspera. Disputes among members go to the host's courts or to private arbitration under a contract. Medical care, insurance and children's schooling follow from the visitors' home countries and whatever the host offers. Money goes through ordinary banks or cryptocurrency exchanges, and each of those is regulated. A permanent site brings planning law, as at Cloverdale in Sonoma County, where a commission paused its review of a 266-acre project in January 2026 over airport noise and safety zones.

The most capable version is a well-organised membership body registered in a stable country, moving among hosts that value the visitors, and holding its records and money under normal law. It offers community, some choice of rules by choice of location, and a route to learning how a group governs itself. It offers no protection from any government once a member is on that government's land, and a host that dislikes the event can end it by refusing visas, cancelling a venue or revoking a licence, as Malaysia's local council did. Recognition, for now, is out of reach for such a group, though a host might choose to sign a memorandum with it.

odds.why: Pop-up cities already happen every year, so building is nearly certain. They have no legal status of their own, so the legal figure is low. Hosts rarely object, and no one needs to board or close anything when nothing is claimed, so holding is high. Moving around does not meet the territory test, and recognition remains very unlikely.

rules.says: Revoked the Network School's business licence, citing breaches of licence conditions and of how the premises could be used.
A state should have a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to enter relations with other states.
Took no land and made no law. Participants stayed under Montenegrin law.

zones.name: Moving voters into a town, then a charter
zones.essay:
In a democracy a small group of new residents can outvote a very small town. The idea is to move enough people to a place to control its government, then use that control to get a charter, which is the founding document of a city, on your own terms. It combines the takeover of a town, a claim inside a state, and a local version of the host's carve-out. In the United States, a city's charter can set its own form of government, though in many states a city has only those powers the state gives it.

The law is clear on the basic steps. Anyone may move, and residents may vote. In the 1982 Antelope vote, Rajneesh's followers had moved in and defeated a plan by older residents to dissolve the town, and that was lawful. The Free State Project gathered about 6,232 movers to New Hampshire by May 2022, and 17 of them held seats in its 400-member House in 2017 to 2018. The Free Town Project in Grafton from 2004 pushed through a 30 percent budget cut in a town of about 1,300. Starbase, Texas, incorporated in May 2025 by a vote under ordinary state rules, with a SpaceX vice-president unopposed as mayor. Nothing about these steps was illegal in itself. A court in the Vernon, California, case in 2006 found that newcomers had received free rent and jobs before registering, and ruled that those actions were not illegal.

Criminal law sets the limit. In 1984 the Rajneeshees poisoned salad bars at ten restaurants with salmonella, sickening 751 people, to lower turnout in county elections, and they bused in upwards of 4,000 homeless people in part to add voters. Those acts led to prosecutions and the end of the commune. Similarly, the state can always respond. The charter itself comes from state law, the state can change that law, and Florida's 2022 and 2023 laws on Reedy Creek show how fast that can happen. California's Assembly voted to dissolve Vernon.

What is open is where the rules stop for a group that moved for a shared purpose. A court may ask whether a person really lives somewhere, and this varies by state and by facts. Reading the record, it seems that a group's shared purpose is not unlawful in itself, and that the questions arise when residence is fake or when a town serves one religion, as in the Kiryas Joel case and at Rajneeshpuram. Americans also disagree about whether a small group should be able to use local rules this way. Older residents of Antelope tried to dissolve their own town to prevent it, and the people who moved said they were using their rights. The Free State Project's own founder, Jason Sorens, at first spoke of a libertarian nation and then backed away from secession.

Follow the sequence. First comes recruitment and a choice of town, which is usually very small because that takes fewer voters. People need housing, jobs and schools for their children, and the shortage of these is what caps the numbers. Then the group contests elections and is met with suspicion and with lawsuits. In Grafton the newcomers' own lawsuits raised town costs. If the group wins, it can change local taxes and zoning, within state law. It cannot change federal law, state criminal law or who issues a passport. Its bonds and contracts remain subject to courts. A mayor of a small town also finds that the state's rules on merging towns, and its tax and police rules, are still in force, as Filettino's mayor did in Italy in 2011. Killington in Vermont voted at a town meeting in 2004 to leave for New Hampshire, and it is still in Vermont.

It has real potential as local politics. A very small group can control a very small town, sometimes for decades. The strongest version moves many households with good reasons to stay, acts within election law, gets a charter under general law, and picks a state that gives its cities broad powers. That can bring local rules on land use, some taxes and the running of services. It cannot bring separation from the country, and it brings neighbours' attention with it.

odds.why: Group moves and local takeovers have happened several times, and Starbase and Antelope show that a vote can make or capture a town. Charter powers depend on state law. Criminal acts ended Rajneeshpuram, and legislatures can change the rules at any time. It stays within the country, so recognition is near zero.

rules.says: Ordinary local governments follow equal voting. Only narrow special districts may limit votes to landowners.
A state may not write a special grant of power for a group defined by religion.

sources.t: Board of Education of Kiryas Joel v. Grumet, 512 U.S. 687 (1994)

zones.name: Buying a bankrupt village or town
zones.essay:
News stories regularly announce that a whole town has been sold. The idea built on this is to buy a failing village, or a government in financial trouble, and thereby acquire the place and the power that runs it. It combines a purchase, a takeover of a town, and a claim inside a state.

What can be bought and what cannot is settled. A town consists of private land parcels, plus a municipal government where one exists. A person can buy all the parcels. A public government has no owner, so no one can buy it. Buford, Wyoming, is the best-known sale. On 5 April 2012 Don Sammons sold it at auction for $900,000 to two Vietnamese men, one later named as Pham Dinh Nguyen. What they bought was about 10 acres of private land with a trading post and gas station, and Buford was an unincorporated community within Albany County, which continued to govern it. The buyer rebranded it PhinDeli Town in 2013, the store was boarded up in 2017, and by 2021 the fuel station was back in business.

Bankruptcy gives no further opening in the United States. Chapter 9 of the federal bankruptcy code is the process for a municipality that cannot pay its debts. Section 109(c) says that an entity may use it only if it is a municipality, is specifically authorised by state law to do so, is insolvent and meets further conditions. In other words the state keeps control over who may enter bankruptcy. A court then helps the municipality adjust its debts, and there is no auction of the government. Other countries respond to failing towns by merging them. Italy in 2011 required towns under 1,000 people to merge with neighbours, which is what led Filettino's mayor to declare a principality in protest, and how towns are organised was still decided by the Italian parliament.

What is open is less about law and more about what a very small population lets an owner do in practice. Owning all the homes in a real municipality, as Vernon's city government did with its housing, gives great influence over who lives and votes there. Whether a new private owner could use this to direct a local government depends on state law on evictions, voting and fair housing. In one Vernon election the city cut off the power of challengers and a judge stepped in. Reading the record, it seems that the combination of very few voters and one landlord is effective, and that it draws state attention once it is noticed.

History does contain true sales of a ruler's rights after money trouble, and they show why the modern version does not work. Before 1699 an imperial commission decided that Schellenberg and Vaduz, whose counts were in debt, should be sold to clear their debts, and the Liechtenstein family bought them. Those were personal lordships, which could be sold under the imperial law of that time. The fief of Sark has also changed hands by sale, and still has a very old structure, yet it answers to the British Crown. In 2010 German politicians suggested that Greece, in its debt crisis, sell islands, and Greece did not. A government in debt might sell land and state companies, while keeping the right to rule.

Follow the steps. A buyer finds an empty village on a listing. It pays for the land, and the sale is entered in the public land register. Any old buildings come with liabilities, and the buyer pays local property tax. The local council, or the county, has planning control. Bringing in residents needs water, sewers and permits, which is why many such villages are empty. A buyer who declares independence, as Seborga's claimant has done since 1963 and Romkerhall's innkeepers have done for tourists, gets publicity and possibly visitors, while the state carries on running the place. A small place that declares it and then refuses taxes faces the same collection system as anyone else.

The potential is modest and real. The strongest version is a group that buys an entire near-empty place in a country with few rules on such purchases, brings in residents, and forms or takes over the local government in a lawful way, using the voters-and-charter route. That gives a physical home, control of planning and a lot of practical freedom. It gives no more legal separation from the country than that route gives.

odds.why: Empty villages are bought regularly, so owning one is easy. Bankruptcy and sale give no governing power, since state law controls municipal status. A buyer owns private land under normal law. Holding means keeping the land, which is safe, but any attempt to act as a government would be stopped.

rules.says: A municipality can use Chapter 9 only with specific state authorisation, and only if insolvent.
Towns under 1,000 people were required to merge with neighbours, which shows that a state decides how towns are organised.

zones.name: A zone held jointly by two states
zones.essay:
A condominium, in international law, is a territory shared and governed by two or more powers at once. It usually settles a quarrel when neither side will give up its claim. The idea here is that two states, perhaps neighbours with a shared problem, could set up a jointly run zone under an authority of their own, with a private project inside it. Each would check the other, and neither alone could cancel it. This combines an international agreement, a buffer between states and a carve-out.

There are many real examples. The New Hebrides were run jointly by France and Britain from 1906 until independence in 1980 as Vanuatu. Neutral Moresnet, 3.5 square kilometres, was run by commissioners from the Netherlands and then Belgium and from Prussia from 1816 to 1920 because both wanted its zinc mine. The mine company dominated daily life, running housing, shops, a hospital and a bank, and residents counted as stateless. Pheasant Island in the Bidasoa river changes hands between Spain and France every six months. The Moselle is a condominium of Germany and Luxembourg. Lake Titicaca's waters were declared an indivisible condominium of Peru and Bolivia. Under a 1973 treaty, Brazil and Paraguay created a binational entity called ITAIPU to run the Paraná River's hydroelectric power, and Argentina and Uruguay share the Río de la Plata's jurisdiction under another treaty of 1973.

Two more modern designs matter most for a project. EuroAirport Basel Mulhouse Freiburg lies in France and has been jointly run by France and Switzerland since a 1946 treaty, with a road allowing passengers to go between Switzerland and the airport without passing French customs. The Nigeria and São Tomé and Príncipe Joint Development Authority was created by a treaty signed on 21 February 2001 to regulate a shared seabed zone thought to hold oil and gas. Its history shows the risks. It raised $300 million in signature bonuses in 2001 yet had funding problems by 2018 and could not pay staff for months, and Nigeria considered withdrawing in 2015.

What is settled is that two states can do this, and that only states can. Treaties between states create the authority, and it carries only what they give it. A private body may run a mine or a dam under such an authority, but it holds no share of the sovereignty. Also settled is that the states can end it together, or that one can leave if the treaty says so. Neutral Moresnet ended when the Treaty of Versailles gave it to Belgium. The Brčko District shows a condominium-type solution within a single country.

What is open is the status of people in such a place. Moresnet's residents were stateless, with no passports of their own, and modern human rights law would treat that differently. No general treaty explains how to handle a condominium's nationality, tax or courts, so each document must say so. Moresnet's mine doctor, Wilhelm Molly, proposed in 1908 turning it into an Esperanto-speaking state called Amikejo, and nothing came of that, and a casino that opened in 1903 closed after pressure from the German emperor. Reading these cases, it seems that the neighbours' joint control gives stability against one of them acting alone, and that it also gives each of them a veto, so that innovations are hard to get.

Follow what a modern founder would meet. Two foreign ministries would need a reason to work together, and a founder's project would rarely be one on its own. Disputes over a border or shared resources are the usual motive, so the founder would be stepping into a quarrel. Each state's parliament would ratify the treaty, and each state's constitution might limit it. Each would also want its police and courts to have some role. Banks would likely want to know whose regulator and whose central bank are responsible. Staff would have the nationality of one or other side, and the two states' laws might conflict. The arrangement can go on unchanged for a long time when both sides are content, and the risk arrives when relations between the two worsen, as a joint authority has no independent force.

The strongest version would be a modest economic zone on a border, under a treaty that gives a joint authority clear legal personality, with a private operator on a long contract. Such a place could offer a mix of rules unavailable in either country, as a bi-national airport does. It would remain the shared property of two states, and it would have two governments to answer to in place of one.

odds.why: Condominiums and joint authorities are real and have lasted a long time, so the law is sound. They exist because two states want them, and a private project has rarely been the reason. Moresnet lasted 104 years with a mining company running daily life. Recognition does not fit, since the two states keep the territory.

rules.says: Created an authority to regulate a shared seabed zone.

rules.cite: Treaty on the Paraná River, 13 August 1973
rules.says: Created ITAIPU as a binational entity run by officials of both countries.

rules.says: France and Switzerland jointly operate an airport on French soil.
