zones.name: Reviving an old title or royal claim
zones.essay:
Now and then someone finds an old paper, a royal line or a forgotten grant and argues that the claim is still alive. The idea combines a claim inside an existing state, an authority kept up from exile, and in some cases a right older than the state. People usually want the old title to stand in for what they lack, which is consent from a government today.

The strongest settled rule comes from the Island of Palmas arbitration, decided on 4 April 1928. An American claim descended from Spain, which said it had discovered the island, lost to the Netherlands, which had actually governed it. The arbitrator, Max Huber, said that discovery gives at most a starting claim, which must be completed by real possession, and that the continuous and peaceful display of the functions of a state is as good as a title. Spain could also pass on only what it really held. Under that reasoning, an old paper counts for little against a government that is running the place today. It is also settled that only states hold title to territory in international law, so a private heir has no court where such a title can be claimed.

The cases follow that rule. Antoine de Tounens declared himself king of Araucania and Patagonia in 1860, with backing from some Mapuche leaders. Chile arrested and expelled him, and in 1873 a Paris court ruled he had not justified his claim to be a sovereign. A line of pretenders has continued in France to this day, including Philippe Boiry from 1951 and Jean-Michel Parasiliti di Para after 2014, and no state deals with them as rulers. David de Mayrena's Kingdom of Sedang of 1888 ended with him in 1890 when France blocked his arms. Seborga's claim that it was left out of the unification of Italy rests on documents said to be in the Vatican's archives, and Italy runs it as an ordinary town. Sealand's claim comes from Roy Bates in 1967. His son Michael and the family sell titles and online citizenship from England, and Britain has said since 1987 that the fort lies within its territorial sea.

Some of this does reach courts, and what happens there is instructive. In Larsen v. Hawaiian Kingdom, a case brought by consent at the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague around 2000, a man sued a person representing the old Kingdom of Hawaii, with the real aim of having American rule declared unlawful. The panel declined. In the absence of the United States, it said, it could neither decide that Hawaii is not part of the United States nor proceed on the assumption that it is not. The Sulu case went further and then failed. Eight people who say they descend from a sultan claimed under an 1878 contract, and a Spanish arbitrator ordered Malaysia to pay $14.92 billion in 2022. The Paris Court of Appeal held in 2023 that he had no power over the dispute, and France's highest court dismissed the heirs' appeal on 6 November 2024. Those heirs were claiming payments and no land.

What is genuinely open lies in a different place. Indigenous claims can rest on real history and on modern rights. The United States Apology Resolution of 1993 said that the overthrow of Hawaii's queen was illegal, and McGirt v. Oklahoma in 2020 held that a reservation still existed because Congress had never ended it. So a government's own past promises can have effect in its own courts. Those are claims within the existing country's law, by peoples with a continuous existence. They give rights and sometimes land. Whether an old treaty can support independence is argued by movements such as the Lakota and some Hawaiian groups, and no court is known to have accepted it. Reading the cases, it seems that an individual's royal descent differs sharply from a people's continuous claim, and that the first has no legal effect while the second can have some.

Follow what happens to a modern claimant. Printing a title or selling honours is usually legal in itself, and selling a passport or a noble title may become fraud if buyers are misled about what they get, as when a Madrid ring sold fake Sealand passports. If the claimant enters the land and acts as ruler, the local police respond, as Chile's did. Tax and criminal laws stay in force. Banks will not hold an account for a government they cannot verify. A claim can bring publicity, and on occasion it has brought harm to others, since the Araucania declaration has been described as a cause of Chile's occupation of Mapuche land.

Its potential lies in culture and in tourism, and for peoples with real history, in litigation over rights. The strongest version would be a claim by a people that has always lived on the land, based on a treaty the state itself signed, pursued in the state's courts. For a private heir, the realistic outcome is an interesting hobby or a family business.

odds.why: Anyone can revive a title on paper, and several families have kept one going for over a century. The Palmas rule favours whoever governs now. The Paris and Hague decisions gave claimants nothing, and the Sulu award was thrown out. Holding counts only because nobody bothers to stop a paper claim. Peoples with real treaties have better prospects than private heirs, but none has gained recognition this way.

rules.says: Discovery gives at most a starting claim. The continuous and peaceful display of the functions of a state is as good as a title.

rules.cite: Larsen v. Hawaiian Kingdom, Permanent Court of Arbitration
rules.says: Without the United States as a party, the tribunal could neither decide that Hawaii is not part of the United States nor assume that it is not.

rules.cite: French Cour de Cassation, 6 November 2024 (Sulu heirs)
rules.says: Dismissed the heirs' appeal because the old contract's clause named an official who no longer exists.

zones.name: A floating zone in a host's waters
zones.essay:
Most people picture a floating settlement far out at sea. A different plan is to float one near shore, inside a country's waters, with that country's agreement and a special legal framework. This combines the territorial sea or the exclusive economic zone with the host's carve-out. It gives up the attempt to escape the coastal state, in exchange for calm water, a nearby port and a government partner.

The law of the sea is clear on the framework. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, or UNCLOS, gives a coastal state sovereignty in its territorial sea, the belt up to 12 nautical miles, or about 22 kilometres, from its coast. Beyond it, out to 200 nautical miles, lies the exclusive economic zone, where Article 60 gives the coastal state the exclusive right to build and to authorise artificial islands and certain installations, and exclusive legal power over them, including customs, tax, health, safety and immigration law. So a host can permit a floating zone and set its rules. Without permission, a long-term structure is at risk. Thailand's navy raided the XLII seastead 14 nautical miles off Phuket in 2019, and Thai officials raised the possibility of the death penalty, on a charge of violating sovereignty.

One gap remains in UNCLOS. It does not define artificial island, and it does not say whether a small floating home on a mooring is an island, an installation or a ship. A structure that stays in place and houses people looks more like what Article 60 covers, but no international court has decided this, and how the XLII case ended is not known. With a host agreement the gap matters less, because the host has already said yes. It matters when a host's successor later changes its mind or when a third country's ship wants to pass.

The real attempts all turned on politics and money. On 13 January 2017 French Polynesia signed a memorandum of understanding with the Seasteading Institute for studies toward seazones with a special governing framework. A memorandum records intentions and usually binds no one. Local people objected, the opposition demanded withdrawal, and in February 2018 the government's position was reported that the deal had no legal force and had expired at the end of 2017. In the Maldives, the government signed with the Dutch developer Dutch Docklands in 2010, and signed again in 2019 and 2022 after a change of government, for a housing project on a 200-hectare lagoon near Malé. Reports differ on how much has been built. At Busan in South Korea, the city, UN-Habitat and the company OCEANIX signed in November 2021 to build a prototype, with about $200 million anticipated and with South Korean law applying to property, police and courts. A local report in October 2023 said no concrete financing had been presented. Kiribati's president spoke in 2011 of floating islands costing about $2 billion, to come from other countries.

What is open, and what has not been tested, is how far a host can go. A country that has authority over its waters could in principle pass a statute giving a floating zone its own commercial law, in the same way as a zone on land. Whether a French territory, for example, could have done so without Paris is something no court has had to decide for this project. Reading UNCLOS, it seems that a coastal state may delegate management inside its waters, and that it cannot pass on its international position, since other states' rights of innocent passage and the coastal state's duties run to the state itself.

Follow the steps. The first is a site study and a set of letters. Next comes a law, which means a public debate, with fishermen and neighbours among those heard. Marine engineers and insurers then want storm data and a classification society's approval, and lenders want the land-law equivalent of a title, which water cannot provide unless the host's law creates one. Boats, ports, medical care and supplies come from the host. A birth or a will on the platform runs under host law, as the host has authority. Environmental review of a lagoon may be the point at which the plan stops. Each change of government reopens the deal, as the Maldives shows.

The most workable version is close to what Busan proposed, which is new floating housing under the ordinary law of a willing host, perhaps with a modest economic zone added. It can answer real needs, particularly for low islands with rising seas, and it can be built with existing engineering at high cost. It gives no separation. A floating city under such an agreement is a neighbourhood of that country, and its residents remain under its law.

odds.why: With a host's consent the legal position is sound, since UNCLOS Article 60 and the territorial sea give the host the power to agree. The French Polynesia deal shows that voters and politics can end it, and Maldives and Busan show slow progress on money. Holding means the host does not cancel. It remains the host's territory, so recognition is very unlikely.

rules.says: A coastal state has sovereignty over its territorial sea, up to 12 nautical miles.
In the exclusive economic zone, the coastal state alone may build or authorise artificial islands and certain installations, and it has exclusive legal power over them.

rules.says: A statement of intent for a special zone. The government said in 2018 that it had no legal force.

zones.name: A treaty regime for a new settled place
zones.essay:
Svalbard is often held up as a place anyone can move to. The idea here is to copy its treaty, in which many countries agree on the status of a place, for some new location, and to combine it with a settlement backed by a state. It would bring together a treaty among many countries, a host's carve-out and the historic state-sponsored colony.

The models need careful statement. In the Svalbard Treaty, signed in Paris on 9 February 1920 and in force from 14 August 1925, Norway's full sovereignty was recognised, on conditions. Citizens and companies of treaty countries have equal rights to live, fish, hunt, mine and do business there. Norway may collect only the tax needed to run Svalbard. Article 9 bans naval bases and fortifications. Russia uses its rights at Barentsburg. The treaty began with 14 parties and had 49 by 2026. Before it, the islands were no state's, and disputes among miners had no court to go to. Nobody there holds a right to rule anything except Norway.

Åland is the second model. In 1921 the League of Nations ruled that Finland keeps sovereignty over these Swedish-speaking islands and must grant them autonomy, and a convention signed on 20 October 1921 made them neutral and demilitarised. Residents have a special right of domicile, needed to vote in Åland's elections and to own rural land, and it is open to Finnish citizens after five years with a knowledge of Swedish. Finland's treaty joining the European Union kept those limits in place. This is the most lasting modern example of a minority gaining strong self-rule under an international settlement. It worked because a state, with an existing people, gave it, under an international body's ruling.

State-backed colonies have a mixed record. In 1928 the Soviet Union allotted land near the Amur River for Jewish settlers, and in 1934 it became the Jewish Autonomous Region, whose status remains in the Russian constitution. Border security was among the reasons, and many settlers left at once. The Jewish population peaked at perhaps 46,000 to 50,000 in the late 1940s and was 837 in 2021. Liberia began as a private American society's colony in 1821, and the United States declined to make it a colony or a protectorate. It became a state, with very heavy loss of life among settlers and conflict with the peoples already there. The Free Territory of Trieste, designed by treaty under the UN Security Council in 1947, was never run as a country, and Italy and Yugoslavia divided it from 1954.

What is settled is that a treaty binds those who join it, and that many states can agree on a status for a place. What is open is whether any place is left for this to happen in. Treaties of this kind arose when land was unclaimed or a dispute needed settling after a war. Marie Byrd Land in Antarctica is unclaimed, and the Antarctic Treaty freezes the claims. The Central Arctic Ocean is sea. Bir Tawil is a by-product of a border argument between Egypt and Sudan. No state has proposed such a treaty for a new settlement in modern times. Reading the texts, it seems that a Svalbard-style deal hands sovereignty to one state on conditions, so its result would be a protected place inside that state, with the settlers as residents.

Follow how it might begin. A founder cannot start this alone, since only states negotiate treaties. There would have to be a crisis or a shared interest, such as climate migration from Pacific countries, and a host offering land. Kiribati's purchase in Fiji shows the current scale, with a state buying land under another state's law and with no treaty at all. Conference diplomacy would then take years, and Svalbard took from before the First World War to 1925 to reach force. Settlers would need a nationality from somewhere, and the conditions in the treaty would need a government to keep them, with the treaty powers able to complain if it did not. Companies could register under rules like those at Svalbard, and banks and ports would follow the sovereign state's law.

The potential lies in something other than founding a country. The strongest version would be an agreement in which a number of states give a displaced or new community a protected place with strong self-rule, as Åland has, on land a willing host provides. For a people in need, that might be worth a great deal. It is unlikely, slow and outside the control of any private group, and sovereignty would stay with the host.

odds.why: Svalbard and Åland show that treaty regimes can last a century. Only states can create them, and no modern example exists for a new settlement. State-backed colonies have a mixed record, as the Jewish Autonomous Region shows. Sovereignty stays with one state in this model, so recognition of a separate country is unlikely.

rules.says: Recognises Norway's sovereignty, with equal rights for nationals of treaty states to live and do business, limited tax, and no naval bases.
The islands are neutral and demilitarised, under Finnish sovereignty, with autonomy required by a League of Nations decision.

zones.name: Buffer or demilitarised land under a treaty
zones.essay:
Buffer zones exist because two sides have stopped fighting without settling who owns what, and a strip of land is kept between them. Some people see these as gaps in the world's map. This route asks whether a treaty could turn such a strip, or a demilitarised area, into a place for a community or a special regime. It combines a buffer zone with international agreement and a host's consent.

The first thing the law settles is that a buffer is not empty of claims. The UN Buffer Zone in Cyprus, 346 square kilometres, was set by ceasefire, and the UN patrols it without owning it, while the claims of the governments on either side continue. Korea's Demilitarized Zone, about 250 kilometres long and 4 wide, comes from the armistice of 27 July 1953. Two villages remain inside it by decision of the armistice committee. Daeseong-dong on the southern side is protected by the United Nations Command, and its 218 residents in 2008 were South Korean citizens who paid no tax and did no military service, on condition that they spend 240 nights a year there. A person arriving there could not join them, since residence descends from pre-war landowners. Pyla in Cyprus is a mixed village in the zone, and about 10,000 people live and farm in the Cyprus zone in all.

A peace treaty can do more. The Israel and Jordan treaty of 1994 recognised Jordanian sovereignty at Baqura, also called Naharayim or the Island of Peace, and it gave Israeli landowners who had held the land since before 1948 a special regime with free entry, under a lease of 25 years, automatically renewed unless one side gave a year's notice. Jordan gave that notice in October 2018 and took full control on 10 November 2019. The Åland Islands are the longest-running peaceful example of demilitarisation. They are neutral under a 1921 convention and part of Finland. The Free Territory of Trieste was the grand design, to be a neutral country under the UN Security Council, and it never got past military governors before Italy and Yugoslavia divided it in 1954.

Now the open points. Nobody has decided whether a third party could administer a demilitarised strip for residents under a new treaty, because no one has asked. In Moresnet and Brčko, a joint regime emerged from a dispute, and each was the work of the parties. Reading the examples, it seems that any such regime needs consent from both of the parties whose quarrel made the buffer. Those parties have often not been able to agree on more basic things. No case has tested whether the UN or another body could accept such a job for a private community.

Follow it step by step. A private group arriving in a UN buffer zone would be stopped by peacekeepers or by the armed forces at the edges. In Korea, the edges of the zone are among the most heavily armed borders in the world. Suppose the two parties wanted a neutral project, say a peace park or a free economic zone. A founder would need both to sign, and a treaty term with an end date or a notice clause, of the kind Jordan used. Investors and insurers would see that one bad year in relations could shut it. Its residents would keep their nationality, its goods would have to pass through one or both sides' customs, and any bank would look to those two states. If the regime ended, private rights would rest on whatever the treaty says. At Baqura, Jordan took full control when the regime ended, whatever the earlier ownership of the land.

The potential is low, and it is tied to peace-making. The strongest version is a treaty that ends a dispute and includes a special area, with clear rights for those already on the land, under a body both sides trust. Such a place could bring real benefit to its people. A founder's role in it would be small, as a contractor or investor at most, and the sovereignty questions would be settled by the two states.

odds.why: Buffers and special treaty areas exist, but they belong to the parties who made them. A newcomer without both sides' consent gets removed. Baqura shows that even a treaty regime can end on one year's notice. A treaty raises the legal figure above that for a plain buffer zone, while recognition stays close to zero.

rules.says: Recognised Jordanian sovereignty over Baqura with a special regime for Israeli landowners, for 25 years, renewable unless one side gave one year's notice.
Each side moved back 2,000 metres. The armistice committee allowed two villages to remain inside.
Made the islands neutral and demilitarised, under Finnish sovereignty.

zones.name: Leased territory with a private operator
zones.essay:
Governments sometimes lease a port or a zone to a foreign company for a very long time. Long terms like 99 years invite people to treat these places as outposts, and a founder might hope for the same. The idea combines a long lease with the purchase route and a carve-out, with a private operator in place of a foreign government. A comparison with the Panama Canal Zone shows the difference between running a port and governing land.

The modern cases are plainly commercial, and that much is settled. In October 2015 the Northern Territory government in Australia gave Landbridge, a privately held Chinese company, a 99-year lease of the Port of Darwin for A$506 million. In July 2017 Sri Lanka's ports authority signed a 99-year lease of Hambantota's port with China Merchants Port for $1.12 billion, through a joint company, with a 15,000-acre economic zone also provided for. Sources give the company's share as either 70 or 85 percent. Neither lease moved sovereignty. Australian and Sri Lankan law still apply. In Laos, the Hong Kong-registered company in the Golden Triangle has 99 years on 10,000 hectares and its own immigration checkpoint, and that is on Lao soil. These leases hand over the operating of a business and a place.

The Canal Zone was a different legal thing. By a convention proclaimed in 1904, the United States received use, occupation and control of a strip of 1,432 square kilometres in perpetuity, and it ran its own governor, police, courts and judges. Panama's grant came straight after the American government had helped it become independent. A private body has never held such powers in modern times. Even that grant ended, with the Torrijos-Carter Treaties of 1977, the end of the zone on 1 October 1979 and of the canal's joint running on 31 December 1999. It had caused riots in 1958, 1959 and 1964. A perpetual text lasted 75 years.

Recent events show how a host can undo a long lease. Reviews in 2021 and 2023 found no grounds to cancel Darwin's lease. In April 2025 the Australian prime minister said the country wanted to buy it back, both main parties promised to return it, and in January 2026 China's ambassador warned against the plan. In May 2026 Landbridge was reported to have filed at ICSID to stop the sale. In Panama, Hutchison's company ran the Balboa and Cristobal ports from the 1990s, and its contract renewed for 25 years in 2021. The Supreme Court ruled the contracts unconstitutional on 29 January 2026, after a suit brought the year before during American pressure on Panama. Reports in February 2026 said the government ordered the ports occupied, and the company has since claimed losses of more than $2 billion in arbitration. In Solomon Islands, the Tulagi deal of 2019 died within weeks because a province had no power to make it.

What is open is first of all about motive. At Hambantota, critics called the lease a debt trap. The payment was mostly used to pay other debts, and scholars including Brautigam and Brown dispute that account, with Brown arguing that China took on more risk and got entangled in local politics. The second open question is how far an international tribunal can reach, as in Darwin. Neither has been resolved. Sri Lanka's foreign minister called the lease a mistake in 2021, and the deal stands.

Follow what a private founder would face. The founder needs serious money first, because these deals cost from hundreds of millions of dollars upward. Next is a bidding process, which is often public, and security reviews at home and in the host. A port needs an operating record, cranes and shipping lines, and insurers will want one. The operator would pay local tax, unless a special law exempts it, employ local people, and follow local customs law. Police and courts remain the host's. People on the land have no new nationality. A home-country government may also be pulled in. The Hutchison sale to a BlackRock-led consortium stalled over objections from the Chinese government, which shows that a company's home state can have a say as well.

The strongest version is what these operators do have. It is a well-capitalised company with a concession under clear law and a treaty behind it, and a host that keeps getting benefits. That gives a long period of operating control over valuable land, and often a say in what is built there. It is a useful commercial position. It is not, and has not been in any modern case, a path to ruling people or leaving the host's legal order. Reading the leases and the rulings, it seems that the longer and larger the lease, the more it draws political attention to its strategic importance.

odds.why: Long commercial leases are common, as Darwin and Hambantota show. They give operating control under the host's law. Panama's court ended a concession in 2026, and Australia is seeking to buy Darwin back, so holding for ten years without state action is far from sure. Money is good because these are working businesses. No such lease has led to recognition.

rules.says: Gave the United States use, occupation and control of a zone in perpetuity. Replaced by treaty in 1977.
Ruled that the laws and acts behind the Panama Ports Company concession contracts were unconstitutional.

rules.cite: Sri Lanka Ports Authority concession, July 2017
rules.says: Leased Hambantota port for 99 years to a joint company with China Merchants Port.
