Panama orders occupation of 2 key canal ports after Supreme Court ruling (AP, headline)
CK Hutchison's PPC says it expands claims against Panama as losses surpass $2b, Shipping Telegraph (headline)

zones.name: Holding land with private soldiers
zones.essay:
Every attempt to claim land eventually meets the question of who will defend it. A group with money can hire armed men, and there is a long history of doing so. The idea combines a takeover, an unrecognised state and a private security or military company as the means of holding ground. The first thing to understand is that the law treats this as a crime in many places, and that it follows people home.

Several rules are clear. In the United States, 18 U.S.C. § 960 says that whoever, within the country, knowingly begins, sets on foot, prepares a means for, furnishes money for or takes part in a military expedition against a foreign state or people with whom the United States is at peace faces a fine and up to three years in prison. This is the descendant of the Neutrality Act of 1794, and it was used in the Gambian coup attempt of 2014. Cherno Nije, a Texas developer who financed the plot, was sentenced to a year and a day, and others to six months or time served. In Britain, the Foreign Enlistment Act 1870 makes it unlawful for British subjects to join forces of a state at war with a state at peace with Britain. South Africa's Foreign Military Assistance Act of 1998 bans citizens and residents from taking part in foreign conflicts without a government committee's approval, and France's 2003 law makes mercenary activity a crime for its citizens, residents and companies.

Internationally, Article 47 of Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, adopted in 1977, says that a mercenary has no right to be a combatant or a prisoner of war, though humane treatment and a trial are still required. The definition requires six things together, including being specially recruited, taking a direct part in fighting and being paid much more than regular soldiers. The UN Mercenary Convention, adopted on 4 December 1989 and in force since 20 October 2001, has a broader rule covering foreigners recruited to overthrow a government for private gain, even if they take no direct part in fighting. Most countries, including the United States and Britain, have not joined it.

The real open question is the line between lawful security and an unlawful force. Hired guards are legal in most places. A private company may guard a mine or a port, and Executive Outcomes, which was founded in South Africa in 1989, had large companies among its clients and worked for the governments of Angola and Sierra Leone. South Africa licensed it under the 1998 act, which suggests that work for a recognised government was treated differently from work against one. Yet whether a guard force holding land for a private founder against a host's police counts as a mercenary or just as criminals depends on the facts and on national law, and few tests exist. The definition is narrow, since all six conditions must be met, and some countries, including the United States, do not endorse it. Reading the text, it seems that a force holding unclaimed land, in the absence of an armed conflict, might not fit Article 47 at all, and that this gives no protection, since ordinary criminal law applies when any state acts.

The history shows a predictable arc. Mike Hoare's force of 1981 went to the Seychelles disguised as rugby players, was detected at the airport and fled in a hijacked plane, and many were tried in South Africa. Bob Denard took over the Comoros with 43 men in 1978 and ran its presidential guard for 11 years, which is the nearest thing to a long success, with outside backing from France and others. He too was forced out. Simon Mann's Wonga Coup plot of 2004 was stopped when Zimbabwean police impounded a Boeing 727 at Harare where weapons were to be loaded. Executive Outcomes retook Sierra Leone's diamond fields in 1995, then withdrew under international pressure. It dissolved on 31 December 1998, the year South Africa's act passed. At Sealand in 1978, hired men took the fort and the family retook it by helicopter, and Germany then called the episode an act of piracy.

Follow the indirect routes. Guns must be bought, and export control laws cover them and the parts, so sellers need licences. Pilots need flight plans, and aircraft are registered in a state. Money for a force moves through banks with reporting duties, and the Wonga plot's payments were later traced through bank records. Recruits are nationals of some country, and their home state may prosecute them. Insurers will not cover an illegal expedition. Once on the land, the group is on someone's territory, and it can be treated as an invading force, with no prisoner of war status. The UN Charter's ban on force protects states, and not a private camp. If a warship arrives at a platform, a private force can do little.

Force has so far brought small groups short periods of control, and it has never brought recognition on its own. The strongest lawful version is a licensed guard company protecting a lawful project with the host's agreement, under the host's law. That is ordinary security. An armed attempt to hold land against a state would mean crimes for everyone involved, from the funder to the driver.

odds.why: Coups and armed claims have been tried many times, and nearly all ended in arrests. Laws in the United States, Britain, South Africa and France reach funders and recruits at home. Denard's long hold of the Comoros needed outside backing and still ended. Money is low because banks and insurers will not touch it. A lawful guard force working under a host's law is possible, and it gains its employer no right to rule.

rules.says: A crime, within the United States, to begin, fund, prepare or join a military expedition against a country at peace with the United States.

rules.cite: Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, Art. 47
rules.says: A mercenary has no right to combatant or prisoner of war status. Six conditions must all be met.
Also covers foreigners recruited to overthrow a government for private gain. Most large states have not joined.

rules.cite: South Africa, Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act 1998
rules.says: Bars private involvement in foreign conflicts without committee approval.

cases.name: Reedy Creek Improvement District
cases.laws: Own building codes and land-use rules under a Florida law
cases.story:
Reedy Creek was a Florida local government built around Walt Disney World. Walt Disney flew over the Orlando area in November 1963, and shell companies then bought land cheaply. In 1966 Disney subsidiaries asked a court to create a drainage district, and on 12 May 1967 Governor Claude Kirk signed the Reedy Creek Improvement Act, which made the district and two cities, one of which was renamed Lake Buena Vista around 1970. A planned living community called EPCOT was the main argument for these powers, and it was never built as a working city.

The district ran land use, building codes, drainage, utilities, roads, fire protection and emergency services. Votes went by land, one per acre, so Disney in effect chose the board, and each supervisor held a five-acre lot. The Florida Supreme Court held in 1968 that the Act did not break the state constitution.

The end came through politics. After Disney opposed a state education law in 2022, the legislature voted to dissolve independent districts formed before November 1968, effective June 2023. Critics noted more than $1 billion in district bonds. In February 2023 the state instead kept the district, renamed it the Central Florida Tourism Oversight District, and gave the governor the appointment of its board. The old board had just signed a development agreement limiting the new board. Disney sued the governor, lost in federal court in January 2024, and settled the state suits in March 2024. The land stayed Disney's and the government passed to the state's appointees.
cases.mechanism: Landowner-elected local government created by a state law

sources.t: Wikipedia: Central Florida Tourism Oversight District

cases.name: Nevada Innovation Zones
cases.story:
Innovation Zones were a 2021 proposal to let technology companies form a new kind of local government in Nevada. The main backer was Blockchains, Inc., which owned about 67,000 acres in and around the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center in Storey County east of Reno. It wanted to break away from the county government and build a smart city, with plans for about 36,000 residents over time. Storey County's population was about 4,000.

Governor Steve Sisolak announced the idea in his State of the State address. The company had given $10,000 to his 2018 campaign and $50,000 to a political committee linked to him. Critics said the plan would allow company towns. Storey County raised logistical and money concerns, and there were questions about where the water would come from. That spring the governor stepped back after he could not persuade lawmakers, and the legislature passed a bill to study the concept. A special committee met twice from August.

In October 2021 the chief executive, Jeff Berns, wrote to the governor withdrawing the request and complaining that the plan had found no champion. He said the company had spent more than $300 million in Nevada and would no longer build a mixed-use city at Painted Rock, though it still planned a technology park. No Innovation Zone was ever created, and no court considered the idea. The case shows the first obstacle to a company district, which is the vote of a legislature, reached before any legal question arises.
cases.mechanism: State law creating a new government on company land

sources.t: Nevada Independent: Blockchains withdraws plan for Innovation Zone legislation

cases.name: City of Vernon
cases.founder: James and Thomas Furlong, John Leonis
cases.story:
Vernon is a city of about five square miles next to Los Angeles, incorporated on 22 September 1905 to promote industry along the railways and later known as exclusively industrial. It added industrial land by annexation while leaving out homes, and in 1932 it voted bonds for its own power plant, and cheap electricity drew large factories. Its population fell from 1,269 in 1930 to about 90 in 1980. The city owned nearly all the housing, and tenants were mostly city workers or people linked to them, paying very low rents. It has fewer than 90 voters by one account, and it reported about 46,000 jobs.

The result was a small electorate that depended on the city for its homes. A firefighter who tried to run for mayor in 1979 was reportedly evicted. In 2006 newcomers moved into a converted office building to contest the council. The city cut off their power and tried to evict them, a judge let them run, and they lost by a landslide. That November charges were filed against the mayor, Leonis Malburg, and others. He was found guilty of fraud, and a former administrator pleaded guilty in 2011 to misusing public money.

In 2011 Assemblyman John Pérez backed a bill to dissolve cities with under 150 residents, which meant only Vernon. The Assembly passed it 58 to 7. Vernon agreed to reforms and to set aside $60 million for nearby cities, and the state Senate rejected the bill on 29 August 2011. New apartments opened to the public in 2015, and the population reached 222 in 2020.
cases.mechanism: A general-law city controlled through ownership of all the housing

cases.name: Pullman, Illinois
cases.story:
Pullman was a company town founded in the 1880s just outside the Chicago city limits by George Pullman's railway car company. About 6,000 employees and as many dependants lived there, in company housing with company markets, a library, churches and entertainment. At their height, more than 2,500 company towns housed about 3 percent of Americans.

During the Panic of 1893 the company cut wages and hours while leaving rents and store prices where they were. That led to the Pullman Strike of 1894. A national commission called the company's paternalism un-American and blamed it partly for the strike. In 1898 the Supreme Court of Illinois ordered the company to give up ownership of the town, which was then annexed to Chicago.

Pullman differs from a special district because the company ruled through ownership and contracts and never held a public charter to govern. It shows that a state court can order a corporation out of the business of owning a town, and that a town built this way can be joined to the neighbouring city once the owner is gone. Later American towns of this type declined from the 1920s, and later law, such as Marsh v. Alabama in 1946, kept constitutional rights in force on company streets that remained.
cases.mechanism: Company ownership of all housing and services

cases.name: Marsh v. Alabama (Chickasaw)
cases.story:
Chickasaw was a suburb of Mobile, Alabama, owned by the Gulf Shipbuilding Corporation. It had houses, streets, sewers, a business block and a post office, and to anyone walking through it looked like any other American town. Marsh, a Jehovah's Witness, stood on the sidewalk near the post office handing out religious literature. The company had posted notices banning such activity without permission. She was told to stop, refused, and was convicted under an Alabama trespass law.

In 1946 the United States Supreme Court reversed the conviction. Alabama argued that the company's rights over its town were the same as a homeowner's rights over guests, and the Court rejected that. It wrote that ownership does not always mean absolute dominion, and that the more an owner opens property for use by the public, the more the owner's rights are limited by the rights of those who use it. People in a company town, it reasoned, have the same need as other citizens to receive information and make decisions.

This is the leading American rule on how far a private town owner's power goes. Anyone planning a private town in the United States meets it first, because a town that functions as a town takes on some of the duties of government. The case limits what a private owner may do inside its land, and it leaves open how far later and different private spaces fall under the same reasoning.
cases.mechanism: Court limit on the rights of a company that owns a town

cases.name: Starbase, Texas
cases.story:
Starbase is a city on the Texas Gulf coast around SpaceX's rocket site at Boca Chica. Elon Musk announced plans for a city called Starbase in March 2021. The Cameron County judge, Eddie Treviño Jr., said that SpaceX must follow all state incorporation rules. A petition to incorporate went to the county in 2024, and voters approved it on 3 May 2025. The city was formed on 20 May 2025 as a Type C general city, with a mayor and two commissioners, and had about 500 people.

Bobby Peden, a SpaceX vice-president, ran unopposed for mayor, and two other residents with ties to SpaceX filled the commission seats without opposition. In February 2026 the commission approved a city police department, and that month it voted in favour of annexing 7,133 acres of unpopulated land, which would bring the city to about 8,000 acres.

Nothing in this is outside ordinary state law. A group of residents followed the state's normal procedure for making a city, and the ties of its officials to one employer did not change the procedure. Federal aviation and environmental law, state law and county roads all remain. The case is the current American example of the simplest form of the idea, in which an employer's workers live in one place and vote themselves into a municipality.
cases.mechanism: Ordinary city incorporation by residents tied to one employer

cases.name: Hawksbill Creek Agreement and Freeport
cases.founder: Wallace Groves, Grand Bahama Port Authority
cases.laws: Bahamian law, with Port Authority licensing and bye-laws
cases.story:
Freeport is a city on Grand Bahama island built under an agreement of 1955 between the government of the Bahamas and Wallace Groves. He received 50,000 acres, with an option on another 50,000, to create a city and free trade zone. The Grand Bahama Port Authority was formed to develop and administer the land, and it planned and built Freeport from nothing. It was exempted from taxes on income, capital gains, real estate and private property until 1985, and later changes extended the agreement to 2054.

The arrangement has lasted 71 years, through Bahamian independence, and its limits were tested in arbitration. The government claimed more than $357 million for 2018 to 2022, for customs, immigration, environmental oversight and regulation in the port area. The Authority counterclaimed for more than $1 billion and argued that it had exclusive authority over the area. A three-member tribunal chaired by Sir Anthony Smellie issued a partial final award reported on 4 March 2026. It rejected the government's claim, because a 1990s review system, under which no new levels had been set, governs the payments. It rejected most of the counterclaims, including the argument for exclusive authority, and it found one breach over environmental bye-laws submitted in 2006, with no damages awarded so far. Both sides claimed victory. Past payments and costs remain unresolved.

This is a private company running a town under a state contract, enforced through arbitration and not through a treaty.
cases.mechanism: A long concession contract to a private port authority

sources.t: Tribune (Bahamas): $357m GBPA claim rejected by tribunal

cases.name: Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe and the Restasis patents
cases.founder: Allergan and the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe
cases.stopped_by: US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit
cases.story:
Restasis is an eye drug made by Allergan. Its patents protected it from cheaper copies, and a competitor, Mylan, challenged them at the United States Patent and Trademark Office through a process called inter partes review, in which a panel of the Office looks again at a patent it granted. Before the hearing, Allergan and the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe of northern New York made an agreement, which Mylan said was meant to shield the patents from review. On 8 September 2017 an assignment transferring the patents to the tribe was recorded. The tribe then moved to end the review on the ground of its sovereign immunity, and Allergan moved to withdraw. The panel refused both.

On 20 July 2018 the Federal Circuit, the appeals court for patent cases, ruled against the tribe. Tribes are immune from suits brought by private parties, the court said, and they are not immune from action by the federal government. It reasoned that the review resembled an agency enforcement action more than a private civil suit, because the director of the Office has wide discretion on whether to start one and the panel can continue even if the parties leave. The Office was acting as a superior sovereign reconsidering its own grant. The court decided only that point, and it left for another day whether a state's immunity is any different.

The case shows that placing an asset with a sovereign partner does not move it out of reach of the federal government that created the right.
cases.mechanism: Transfer of patents to a tribe to claim immunity from review

sources.t: Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals (Fed. Cir. 2018), National Indian Law Library copy

cases.name: Big Picture Loans and rent-a-tribe lending
cases.founder: Lac Vieux Desert Band and Matt Martorello
cases.story:
The Lac Vieux Desert Band of Lake Superior Chippewa Indians entered online lending in 2011 through a tribally owned company, Red Rock Lending, with help from a company owned by an outside investor, Matt Martorello. After an adverse Second Circuit ruling and a federal enforcement action against another lender claiming tribal ties, the tribe restructured the business into Big Picture Loans and Ascension Technologies and bought Martorello's company in a seller-financed deal. Under it the tribe first received 2 percent of gross revenue, later 3 percent. By September 2017 about $20 million had gone to a company connected to the investor and nearly $5 million to the tribe.

Virginia borrowers sued, saying the loans broke state law. A district court found that the structure was set up mainly to help the investor avoid liability and denied immunity. On 3 July 2019 the Fourth Circuit reversed. It agreed that the company claiming immunity must prove it, and it adopted factors on creation, purpose, control, intent and financial relationship. It said there is no rule that a tribe must get a set share of revenue, and it held both companies to be arms of the tribe. Federal court records later included a finding, reported in 2020, that facts had been misrepresented to the Fourth Circuit.

The Second Circuit took a different path in Gingras v. Think Finance on 24 April 2019. There a tribe's officers could be sued for orders stopping violations of state law off tribal land, and the loans' arbitration clauses were found unenforceable. The two rulings are about different claims, so they do not directly clash, and together they show what a tribal partnership can and cannot cover.
cases.mechanism: Lending through tribally owned companies under tribal law

sources.t: Williams v. Big Picture Loans (4th Cir. 2019), National Indian Law Library copy
Consumer Law and Policy Blog: Gingras v. Think Finance (2d Cir. 2019)
Turtle Talk: Federal court finds factual misrepresentations made to Fourth Circuit in Williams v. Big Picture Loans (headline)

cases.name: Bay Mills casino at Vanderbilt
cases.story:
The Bay Mills Indian Community runs a casino on its reservation under a compact with Michigan, which is what federal gaming law requires for casino games on Indian lands. In 2010 it opened a second gaming site in Vanderbilt, a small village in Michigan's Lower Peninsula about 125 miles from the reservation. It bought the property with interest from a federal fund that Congress had created to compensate the tribe for 19th-century takings of land, and it argued that this purchase made the property Indian land. The Interior Department concluded that it did not, and Michigan sued to close the casino.

In 2014 the United States Supreme Court ruled for the tribe on immunity, though not on the land. The gaming law removes immunity only for gaming on Indian lands, and the state's own case was that this casino was off them, so no exception applied. The Court also refused to overturn its earlier decision in Kiowa, which had extended immunity to off-reservation business. It said that limiting the immunity is the job of Congress.

The Court pointed out what the state could still do. On its own land a state has more power, it said, and it can bring actions against the responsible individuals. The opinion is the clearest statement of how much protection a tribal partner can bring and where the protection stops. The state's right to pursue people, and to enforce its law on its own land, continues even when it cannot sue the tribe.
cases.mechanism: Tribal immunity for off-reservation business

sources.t: Michigan v. Bay Mills Indian Community (U.S. 2014)

cases.name: Micula v Romania
cases.founder: The Micula claimants and their companies
cases.story:
The Micula case began with a tax break. With effect from 1 April 1999, Romania adopted an investment incentive scheme for certain regions, known as EGO 24. In the early 2000s the claimants built a large, integrated food production business in the region, relying on the scheme. In 2002 Romania and Sweden signed a treaty protecting each other's investors and allowing arbitration at ICSID.

Then Romania began joining the European Union, which it did on 1 January 2007. The EU told it that schemes like EGO 24 broke the rules against state aid, meaning government subsidies that distort competition. Romania repealed nearly all the incentives. On 28 July 2005 the claimants asked for arbitration. On 11 December 2013 the tribunal ruled that Romania had breached the treaty and awarded about £70 million plus interest, and Romania's attempt to annul the award failed.

Romania's partial payment led to a clash between two legal systems. On 26 May 2014 the European Commission ordered it to stop, and on 30 March 2015 it decided that paying the award would be illegal state aid. The European General Court annulled that decision on 18 June 2019 because the Commission had applied its powers to events before Romania joined. The Commission appealed. On 19 February 2020 the United Kingdom Supreme Court unanimously lifted a stay so that the award could be enforced there. Later rulings in Europe continued the dispute, with one blog reporting the General Court again treating the award as state aid.

The case shows that a repealed incentive can cost a state money, and that collecting takes many years and may run into another legal order.
cases.mechanism: Treaty arbitration over a repealed regional incentive scheme

sources.t: UK Supreme Court press summary: Micula v Romania [2020] UKSC 5
Kluwer Arbitration Blog: Yet another chapter in the Micula saga (headline)

cases.name: Cook Islands and Niue in free association
cases.founder: New Zealand, the Cook Islands and Niue
cases.recognition: Sign UN treaties and join UN bodies, not UN members
cases.story:
The Cook Islands and Niue are Pacific places that run themselves in free association with New Zealand, the Cook Islands since 4 August 1965 and Niue since 19 October 1974. New Zealand cannot legislate for them. It acts on defence and foreign affairs only when their governments ask and with their consent. They manage their own immigration, and they have no citizenship of their own, since their people are New Zealand citizens. Their constitutions, a 1983 exchange of letters and a 2001 joint declaration describe the relationship.

They have gradually taken on the outward signs of a country. Both sign UN treaties and join UN bodies as states, the Cook Islands from 1992 and Niue from 1994. They are still not UN members. In 2025 Prime Minister Mark Brown of the Cook Islands said the UN had confirmed that his country did not meet membership requirements, and Foreign Minister Tingika Elikana said joining would need a referendum and a new look at the tie to New Zealand. He also spoke of a new constitutional agreement reflecting growing independence. A New Zealand foreign ministry spokesperson said that the Cook Islands is not a fully independent and sovereign state, and New Zealand has said that UN membership could cost its people automatic access to New Zealand citizenship.

The status of these places is therefore argued by the governments concerned. They show that a small place can act internationally for decades without a seat at the UN, and that access to a larger partner's passport may be what holds it back from going further.
cases.mechanism: Self-government with a larger state's help on defence and foreign affairs

cases.name: Chagos treaty of 2025
cases.story:
The Chagos Archipelago is a group of islands in the Indian Ocean. In 1965, before Mauritius became independent, Britain separated it from Mauritius to create the British Indian Ocean Territory. The Prime Minister told the Mauritian premier he could go home with independence or without it, and the Mauritian side accepted detachment for £3 million and promises that the islands would return when no longer needed. About 1,360 people lived there at the time. The UN General Assembly had asked Britain not to divide Mauritius, by a vote of 89 to none.

In February 2019 the International Court of Justice advised, 13 to 1, that decolonisation had not been lawfully completed and that Britain should end its administration as rapidly as possible. The court held that Mauritius could not validly consent to the detachment while under British authority, and that the separation had not rested on the free and genuine will of the people.

On 22 May 2025 the two prime ministers signed an agreement. Mauritius would hold sovereignty over the whole archipelago and would authorise Britain to use its rights over Diego Garcia, the site of a military base, for an initial 99 years, for annual payments. The United States, India and the African Union welcomed it, while the Conservatives, Reform UK and some Chagossians objected. In February 2026 a group of Chagossians landed on Île du Coin. Ratification stalled that year, as Britain said a change in the American president's position prevented updating the 1966 British and American agreement. The implementing bill lapsed in April 2026, and as of October 2026 the treaty had not entered into force.
cases.mechanism: Transfer of sovereignty with a 99-year right to use one island

cases.name: ICRC and Swiss headquarters agreement
cases.founder: International Committee of the Red Cross and Switzerland
cases.recognition: Recognised as having international personality by Switzerland
cases.story:
The International Committee of the Red Cross is based in Geneva, and on 19 March 1993 it signed a headquarters agreement with the Swiss Federal Council at Berne, taking effect at once. It is an example of a body founded privately that gained a state's written recognition of its standing, so it is a useful marker for how far this kind of deal can go.

Under Article 1, Switzerland recognises its international juridical personality and its legal capacity. Under Article 3, no Swiss public official may enter its premises without its express consent. Under Article 5, it has immunity from legal process and from execution, except where its president formally waives it, in civil claims over its vehicles, in staff disputes and in counter-claims tied to its own proceedings. Article 6 exempts it from most direct and indirect taxes.

The host kept some things. Non-Swiss staff stay in part of the Swiss social insurance system under Article 12, and Article 13 leaves them liable for civil claims from vehicle use and for road traffic fines. Article 20 says Switzerland bears no international responsibility for what the organisation or its staff do. Article 21 gives the foreign ministry the job of carrying out the agreement.

The agreement protects an organisation in order to allow it to do its work. It gives the body no territory and no people. Its staff are ordinary residents and nationals of their own countries, within the limits listed.
cases.mechanism: Immunity and inviolable premises by agreement with a host

sources.t: Agreement between the ICRC and Switzerland, 1993 (ICRC Casebook)

cases.name: Jam v. International Finance Corporation
cases.story:
The International Finance Corporation is a World Bank institution based in Washington. It lent money to Coastal Gujarat Power Limited to build a coal-fired power plant in Gujarat, India. People living nearby, led by Budha Ismail Jam, sued it in the United States and said pollution from the plant harmed their air, land and water. The lower courts held that it was immune.

The question was what a 1945 American law meant by saying international organisations have the same immunity as foreign governments. In 1945 foreign governments had nearly total immunity. Since 1952 and a 1976 law they have had a narrower immunity, which leaves them open to suit over commercial activity. On 27 February 2019 the Supreme Court ruled by seven votes to one that the law means today's immunity, so that organisations and foreign governments stay on the same footing. Justice Breyer dissented.

The Corporation warned that this would expose development banks to lawsuits over their main work. The Court called that concern inflated. It noted that the law only provides default rules and that an organisation's charter can say something different. It did not decide whether this particular suit could go forward under the commercial activity rule.

The case matters for anyone taking headquarters immunity as a model. Immunity comes from a statute or a charter and can shift with the law, and a body that does business may have much less of it than its founding documents suggest.
cases.mechanism: Limits on the immunity of international organisations in US courts

cases.name: Monaco's data embassy in Luxembourg
cases.story:
On 15 July 2021 the Luxembourg government signed an agreement with the Principality of Monaco to create a data centre on Luxembourg territory for Monaco's exclusive use. Luxembourg's parliament endorsed it by vote on 9 November 2022. A data embassy is a data storage space held in another country, which comes with protections borrowed from diplomatic law, such as the inviolability of the premises and of the data.

The premises are exempt from search, requisition, attachment or execution. No official or person exercising public authority in Luxembourg, whether administrative, judicial, military or police, may enter without prior approval from Monaco's authorised representative, except in an emergency such as a fire. Monaco chose Luxembourg for its political stability and for the security of its data storage. The report on the law describes this as the third data embassy based in Luxembourg, after those of the European Patent Organisation and Estonia.

Monaco is a tiny state that wanted protected copies of its records in another country. The arrangement took about 16 months from signature to parliamentary approval, and it passed through the host's ordinary law-making. Only recognised states and an organisation made up of states are known to have such arrangements in Luxembourg. A body without recognition would have no standing to sign the same kind of document.
cases.mechanism: Treaty giving diplomatic-style protection to a state's data centre abroad

sources.t: DLA Piper: New Monaco data embassy in Luxembourg (2022)

cases.name: Kiryas Joel and its school district
cases.story:
Kiryas Joel is a village in New York whose people are Satmar Hasidim, who practise a strict form of Judaism. Its founders drew its boundaries under New York's general village incorporation law so as to take in only Satmars. Its children attended religious schools, but children with disabilities needed special public services, and the village fell within the Monroe-Woodbury Central School District. In 1989 New York's legislature passed Chapter 748, a special statute that carved out a separate public school district following the village's lines.

Taxpayers sued, and in 1994 the United States Supreme Court ruled the statute unconstitutional under the First Amendment's bar on establishing a religion. Justice Souter said the district had not received its authority as one of many communities eligible under a general law, so there was no assurance that the next religious community would get the same treatment. Four justices also said that handing state authority over public schools to a group defined by common religion brought about a fusion of government and religion, comparing the case to Larkin v. Grendel's Den. The Court pointed out that other means of serving those children existed.

The decision did not overturn the village, which was formed under the general law. The case therefore draws a line between a community that uses general rules open to anyone and a government that writes a special law for one faith. Founders of a religious community meet that line whenever they ask a legislature for something of their own.
cases.mechanism: A special school district drawn around a religious village

sources.t: Board of Education of Kiryas Joel v. Grumet, 512 U.S. 687 (1994)

cases.name: Colorado City and Hildale
cases.challenge: State land action 2007, federal suit 2012, jury verdict 2014
cases.story:
Colorado City, Arizona, founded as Short Creek in 1913, lies on the Utah line next to Hildale. It became home to a polygamist branch of Mormonism, the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints. A police raid in 1953 did not end the community. The town incorporated in September 1985, and most property was held by a church real estate trust called the United Effort Plan.

Under the leader Warren Jeffs, some 20 men were expelled in January 2004, and an estimated 400 young men were pushed out from 2001 to 2006. Jeffs was arrested on 28 August 2006. In 2007 state authorities began dismantling church ownership of the land. On 6 April 2010 county officials served search warrants on town officials over misuse of funds, and the Hildale public safety department was shut down.

In July 2012 the United States Justice Department sued, alleging that Colorado City's government, including its police, was taking orders from the church. Arizona's attorney general funded daily sheriff's patrols. On 20 March 2014 a jury in a private suit, Cooke v. Colorado City, found that the towns had discriminated against a family because they were not members and awarded $5.2 million. The town's population fell from 4,821 in 2010 to 2,478 in 2020.

This is the American example of a religious group holding both a town's land and its government for decades, and of the government eventually moving in through a land trust case, criminal charges and civil rights lawsuits.
cases.mechanism: A religious land trust and control of a town's officials

cases.name: Shanghai International Settlement
cases.recognition: Recognised by treaty powers, on Chinese territory
cases.story:
The Shanghai International Settlement was a district of Shanghai governed for nearly a century by foreign residents. After Britain's victory in the First Opium War, the Treaty of Nanking opened five Chinese ports, including Shanghai, and Land Regulations agreed in 1845 between a Chinese official and the British consul set the first British settlement. In 1854 Western businessmen formed the Shanghai Municipal Council, against consular protests. New Land Regulations of 11 July 1854 said in Article 28 that the land remained Chinese territory, subject to China's sovereign rights.

The council ran police, fire services, public works and, by the 1880s, utilities. Foreign taxpayers elected it, and property requirements meant only about 3 percent of the population could stand. Chinese residents could not join until 1928. Foreigners from treaty powers fell under their own national laws and consular courts, while Chinese people went before a Mixed Court from 1864 and later other courts. A Volunteer Corps served as a reserve, and a British battalion arrived in 1927. The area reached 5,584 acres by 1899 and 22.59 square kilometres by 1925, with 1,137,298 people that year.

It ended through war and treaties. Japanese troops occupied it on 8 December 1941. In February 1943 Britain and the United States gave up their rights by treaty, and in July 1943 Japan handed the council to a pro-Japanese Chinese government. It was the most developed case of private citizens running a city under a foreign treaty, and it depended on unequal treaties and on the armed force of the powers that imposed them.
cases.mechanism: Self-government by foreign taxpayers under unequal treaties

cases.name: Romer's charter cities
cases.story:
A charter city is an idea made popular by the American economist Paul Romer in a 2009 TED talk. Romer argued that poor countries could change their growth path through better rules and that rules are easier to change in a new place. In his model, a host country gives responsibility for a charter city to a more developed country, which acts as a trustee, so that new rules can emerge, and people decide whether they like the rules by choosing whether to move there. Critics called the arrangement neo-colonial.

Honduras took up the idea. The government considered Zones for Employment and Economic Development, without a third-party government overseeing them. Romer chaired a transparency committee for the project and resigned in September 2012, after the agency in charge signed agreements with international developers without involving the committee. An earlier version of the Honduran law was struck down as a breach of sovereignty, and the 2013 ZEDE law then took its place until the courts struck that down too in 2024.

Romer later became a critic of what followed. In 2025 he told Bloomberg that Próspera's developers had lost their way and that it was like a gated community, and that it was not even close to what anyone would recommend as a model for helping a country develop. The trustee feature of his design has never been used, so whether a foreign government would agree to run a city in another country under a charter remains untested.
cases.mechanism: A host hands a new city to a foreign trustee government

sources.t: Bloomberg Law: Libertarian city dream in Honduras becomes $11 billion nightmare

cases.name: Sale of Buford, Wyoming
cases.founder: Don Sammons, later Pham Dinh Nguyen
cases.story:
Buford is an unincorporated community in Albany County, Wyoming, sometimes described as a ghost town. Don Sammons owned about 10 acres there from 1992, including the Buford Trading Post and its gas station. He decided to sell in order to move closer to his adult son, and on 5 April 2012 the property went to auction. Two Vietnamese men, at first unidentified and one later named as Pham Dinh Nguyen, won with a bid of $900,000.

News stories said a town had been sold. What was sold was private land and a business. Buford had no municipal government to transfer, because it is an unincorporated community and Albany County governs it. The 2020 census recorded a population of zero.

The new owner rebranded the site PhinDeli Town Buford in 2013. In September 2017 the manager resigned and the store was boarded up. By August 2021 the fuel station and mini-market were operating again, and in 2024 the owner announced a diesel fuel island. In 2026 the market was using the name Buford Trading Post Office.

The sale is a clean example for anyone who imagines buying a town. It brought ownership and a business, along with the county's taxes and rules, and it brought no public powers at all.
cases.mechanism: Private sale of all the land in an unincorporated place

cases.name: Nigeria and São Tomé Joint Development Authority
cases.founder: Nigeria and São Tomé and Príncipe
cases.recognition: Created by treaty between two states
cases.story:
Nigeria and São Tomé and Príncipe share a maritime border in the Bight of Bonny, in West Africa, where the seabed is thought to hold oil and gas. Instead of fighting over a boundary, they signed a treaty in Abuja on 21 February 2001 on the joint development of petroleum and other resources. It set up a Joint Development Zone and an authority to regulate it, with a head office in Abuja.

Two states thus created a small body to run a resource area that neither would rule alone. The zone has a body of staff and a budget, and a licensing process, with the last round held in 2004. The authority collected a total of $300 million in signature bonuses, payments companies make on signing a contract, in the early years.

Later reports are less encouraging. In 2013 the bill for its headquarters building was reported to be inflated. In 2015 Nigeria considered withdrawing, saying it had paid the bills for the previous five years and that the expected $100 million a year was not materialising. In 2016 the budget was about $12 million a year, and there were allegations of financial irregularities. By 2018 it could not pay staff for months. In 2019 the international transparency body EITI asked again for a reconciliation of revenues.

The example shows that a treaty can create a jointly run area quickly, and that its survival depends on income and on the continuing will of both sides, particularly the larger one.
cases.mechanism: Two states run a shared resource zone through a joint authority

sources.t: Wikipedia: Nigeria–São Tomé and Príncipe Joint Development Authority

cases.name: Larsen v. Hawaiian Kingdom
cases.story:
Larsen v. Hawaiian Kingdom was an arbitration at the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague, around 2000. Hawaii was an independent kingdom until the overthrow of its queen in 1893 and annexation by the United States in 1898, and many Hawaiians consider both illegal. Lance Paul Larsen brought a case against a man named Sai, who claimed to represent the Hawaiian Kingdom, and said that the kingdom had failed to protect his rights as a subject. Since both agreed to arbitrate, the case could proceed.

The real goal, according to accounts of the case, was to have United States rule in Hawaii declared a breach of treaty obligations and of international law. The United States was not a party. The panel said that this left it with no dispute it could decide. In the panel's words, in the absence of the United States, the tribunal could neither decide that Hawaii is not part of the USA, nor proceed on the assumption that it is not, because to do either would disregard a principle going to the heart of the arbitral function in international law.

The case is sometimes quoted as though the Court had recognised the kingdom. The panel's words show otherwise, since it refused to assume anything on that question. The lesson is procedural. Two parties can agree to arbitrate almost anything, and the result binds only them. A state that stays out cannot be bound, and no ruling about its territory can result from a case it did not join.
cases.mechanism: Arbitration between two private parties on the status of a state

cases.name: Åland settlement of 1921
cases.founder: League of Nations, Finland and Sweden
cases.story:
Åland is an archipelago between Finland and Sweden whose people speak Swedish. A convention of 30 March 1856 had already barred Russia from fortifying the islands, and in 1916 Russia did so anyway, alarming Sweden. After Finland became independent, Ålanders' wish to join Sweden became a dispute, and in 1921 the League of Nations ruled that Finland kept sovereignty and must grant the islands political autonomy.

Finland had passed an autonomy act dated 7 May 1920, replaced by new acts in 1951 and 1991. On 20 October 1921 Sweden, Finland and several other European countries signed a convention that guaranteed the islanders' rights to their language, culture and traditions and made Åland a neutral and demilitarised zone. The first regional assembly met on 9 June 1922.

Swedish is the only official language. A right of domicile passes from parent to child, and an immigrant may apply after five years with Finnish citizenship and enough Swedish. That right is needed to vote in Åland's parliamentary elections, to stand for them or to own rural land. A protocol to Finland's EU accession treaty lets Åland keep those limits, and Åland held its own referendum on joining in 1994.

The settlement is one of the longest-lasting examples of a treaty-backed autonomy. It gave a real community strong self-rule and control of who may hold land. It did this inside an existing state, by a decision of an international body, and the islands remained Finnish.
cases.mechanism: Autonomy required by an international ruling, under a treaty of neutrality

cases.name: Jewish Autonomous Region
cases.story:
Birobidzhan is the capital of Russia's Jewish Autonomous Oblast, near the Amur River on the Chinese border. A Soviet decree of 28 March 1928 allotted the land to settle Jewish workers, and on 7 May 1934 it became the Jewish Autonomous Region within Soviet Russia. Two reasons are given. It offered Soviet Jews, among whom unemployment had passed 30 percent in 1924, a settlement as an alternative to Zionism, and it strengthened a thinly held frontier. Pavel Sudoplatov, a Soviet intelligence official, is cited as saying that Stalin ordered it as a border outpost and not as a favour to Jews.

Settlement began badly. In spring 1928, 654 Jews came, and by October about half had left. The Jewish population reached about 20,000 in 1937, was 17,695 in 1939 and peaked at about 46,000 to 50,000 in the late 1940s, roughly a quarter of the region. About 1,200 came from outside the Soviet Union. It then fell to 14,269 in 1959, 8,887 in 1989, about 1,600 in 2010 and 837 in 2021, when it was 0.6 percent of the population.

Legally it survived, and Article 65 of the Russian Constitution still lists it as Russia's only autonomous oblast. Its charter of 1997 recognises Yiddish as a minority language. The case shows that a powerful state can create a homeland by decree, including a legal status that outlasts the original people, and that a legal status alone does not keep settlers in a place.
cases.mechanism: A state decree creating an autonomous homeland

cases.name: Naharayim and Baqura
cases.story:
Naharayim, known in Jordan as Al-Baqoura and sometimes as the Island of Peace, lies where the Jordan and Yarmouk rivers meet. In 1927 Pinchas Rutenberg signed an agreement with King Abdullah I to build a hydroelectric station there, and its channels and dams, with the rivers, made an artificial island. Power generation started in 1932 and stopped after the 1948 war. The land along the river was under Jewish ownership from before the State of Israel.

The peace treaty between Israel and Jordan in 1994 dealt with this through a special regime. It recognised Jordanian sovereignty, and it gave the Israeli landowners free entry. Jordan leased the land back, so that farmers from Kibbutz Ashdot Ya'akov could keep working it, for a term of 25 years. The lease renewed automatically, and Jordan could end it with one year's notice. Israeli tourists could enter with identity cards at a gate, with no visa, and from 2012 only in groups with an authorised guide.

Jordan announced in October 2018 that it would end the arrangement, giving the notice required. On 10 November 2019 it took full control, and King Abdullah II said that Jordan was asserting full sovereignty over every inch of those lands.

The case is a clear example of how a treaty can create private access across a border in a sensitive place, and of how a notice clause leaves the host able to end it. Private ownership did not stop the end of the regime.
cases.mechanism: A treaty lease-back with private access in a border area

cases.name: Port of Darwin lease to Landbridge
cases.challenge: Reviews 2021 and 2023, buy-back plan 2025, ICSID filing 2026
cases.story:
The Port of Darwin is in Australia's Northern Territory. In late 2014 and early 2015 the territory's government invited offers, and 33 companies signalled interest. In October 2015 Landbridge, privately held and based in Rizhao, China, won a 99-year lease for A$506 million, more than 25 times the port's profit over the previous two years, and promised to invest A$200 million over 25 years. Its owner, the billionaire Ye Cheng, has close ties to the Chinese Communist Party, and the port lies near a base used by United States Marines and an airport with military use.

A senior defence official raised concerns in 2015. A review in 2021 found no national security grounds to overturn the lease, and in October 2023 the federal government said it would not cancel it. In April 2025 Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Australia sought to buy back the port, and both main parties promised during the election campaign to return it to Australian ownership. The former chief minister, Adam Giles, defended his decision. China's ambassador criticised the plan, and in January 2026 warned that nationalising the port would harm trade and relations.

In May 2026 Landbridge was reported to have filed at the World Bank's arbitration centre, ICSID, seeking to halt what is described as a forced sale. How that will end is not known.

The case shows that a territory's government can grant a long lease, that security arguments can return ten years later, and that the operator's remaining protection may lie in a treaty claim.
cases.mechanism: A 99-year commercial lease of a port to a foreign company

cases.name: Hambantota port lease
cases.founder: China Merchants Port and Sri Lanka Ports Authority
cases.story:
Hambantota is a port in southern Sri Lanka. In December 2016 Sri Lanka announced plans to lease it to China Merchants Port, and the agreement was signed in July 2017, replacing an earlier one that the new government had rescinded. The ports authority formed the Hambantota International Port Group, and a lease was granted for 99 years. China Merchants was to pay $1.12 billion and spend more on developing the port. The deal also provided for a 15,000-acre special economic zone. Available accounts give its stake as 70 percent or 85 percent.

The agreement was delayed by worries that the port could be used for military purposes, and India and the United States worried about Chinese control in the Indian Ocean. Critics called it debt-trap diplomacy, based on the size of the loans, Sri Lanka's trouble paying them and the 99-year term. Others dispute that. The money went into dollar reserves and paid short-term debts to non-Chinese creditors, unrelated to the port. Brautigam, writing in 2019, calls the debt-trap story a meme needing scrutiny, and Brown, writing in 2023, argues that China committed more money and took on more risk and became entangled in local politics.

In February 2021 Sri Lanka's foreign minister Dinesh Gunawardena called the lease a mistake by the previous government. As of at least 2024 the port was not a major commercial success, though shipping was increasing. Sri Lanka's law continues there, and the case is mainly a dispute about how a state came to need such a deal.
cases.mechanism: A 99-year concession through a joint company

cases.name: Panama Ports Company ruling
cases.story:
Panama Ports Company, a subsidiary of Hong Kong's CK Hutchison, has run the container ports of Balboa on the Pacific side of the Panama Canal and Cristóbal on the Atlantic side since the 1990s. Its contract renewed automatically in 2021 for another 25 years. The canal carries an estimated 5 percent of world maritime trade, and the United States handed the canal itself to Panama in 1999.

At the start of 2025 President Donald Trump threatened to take control of the canal, saying it was in effect under Chinese control. CK Hutchison announced that it would sell dozens of ports, including these two, to a group led by BlackRock for nearly $23 billion, and the deal appeared to stall after objections from China. A lawsuit filed in 2025 said that the contracts rested on unconstitutional laws. An audit reported accounting errors said to have cost Panama about $300 million since the extension.

On the evening of 29 January 2026 Panama's Supreme Court announced that the laws and acts underpinning the contracts were unconstitutional. The company denied all the allegations and said the ruling lacked legal basis. China said it would take necessary measures to protect its companies. Headlines in February 2026 reported that the ruling was finalised, that Panama ordered the two ports occupied, and later that the company had expanded its claims against Panama with losses above $2 billion.

The case shows that a court can end a port concession of nearly 30 years in one judgment, and that the operator then turns to arbitration for money.
cases.mechanism: A long port concession ended by a constitutional court

sources.t: Al Jazeera: Panama court rules Chinese control of canal ports unconstitutional (Jan 2026)
Panama orders occupation of 2 key canal ports after Supreme Court ruling (AP, headline)
CK Hutchison's PPC says it expands claims against Panama as losses surpass $2b, Shipping Telegraph (headline)

cases.name: Executive Outcomes
cases.story:
Executive Outcomes was a private military company founded in South Africa in 1989 by Eeben Barlow, a former South African Defence Force officer, and Michael Mullen, as apartheid was ending and many soldiers were leaving. It recruited many former special forces men, and at its peak employed about 2,000 former soldiers. Clients were said to include large oil and mining companies and the governments of Angola, Sierra Leone and Indonesia. Several details of its history are disputed.

In Angola it trained and then fought for the government against UNITA, after UNITA rejected the 1992 election. Under pressure from the UN and the United States the government ended the contract. In Sierra Leone in March 1995 it contained the Revolutionary United Front insurgency and regained control of the diamond fields, and it forced a negotiated peace. The government then yielded to international pressure to have it withdraw. Later fighting took the rebels into the capital.

South Africa's Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act of 1998 prohibited direct participation as a combatant for private gain, and required official approval for military help abroad. The company gave input on the bill and was issued a licence. It was dissolved on 31 December 1998. A company with the name was said to have been re-established in November 2020.

For anyone thinking of private force as a way to hold land, this is the most capable example, and its military contracts were for recognised governments. Even then its presence depended on foreign approval, and it had no claim to the land itself.
cases.mechanism: Hired military force working for recognised governments

cases.name: Gambian coup attempt and the Neutrality Act
cases.founder: Cherno Nije, Njaga Jagne, Lamin Sanneh and others
cases.challenge: US prosecutions under the Neutrality Act, 2015 onward
cases.story:
On 30 December 2014 gunfire broke out in Banjul, the capital of The Gambia. A small group led by Lieutenant Colonel Lamin Sanneh, a former commander of President Yahya Jammeh's guard, and Njaga Jagne, a Gambian-American captain in the Kentucky National Guard, tried to overthrow the president while he was abroad. It failed, and four people died, including Sanneh and Jagne. Jammeh returned the next day.

The plot was prepared largely in the United States. Cherno Nije, a developer in Texas, put up the money, with an initial budget of $200,000 and a later figure of $221,000. Banka Manneh in Georgia made introductions, and Papa Faal and Alagie Barrow helped with recruits and buying weapons. FBI raids began on 1 January 2015 in Georgia, Kentucky, Minnesota and Texas.

Those men were charged under a modern form of the Neutrality Act of 1794, now 18 U.S.C. § 960, which makes it a crime within the United States to begin, prepare, fund or take part in a military expedition against a country at peace with the United States. Faal, Barrow and Manneh pleaded guilty. Nije received a year and a day, Barrow and Manneh six months each, and Faal time served.

The case shows how the law reaches a private armed attempt at the point of departure.
cases.mechanism: A coup plot funded from abroad, prosecuted at home
